c-068.principle: DEET (N,N-diethyl-m-toluamide, $\mathrm{C_{12}H_{17}NO}$) disrupts mosquito odor receptors so they cannot locate you. Higher concentration lasts longer, but the benefit levels off.
c-068.example: 30% DEET typically protects ~6 hours and 10% ~2 hours; above 50% adds little. Apply from your hands, not sprayed on the face, and do not use on babies under 2 months.
c-068.actionItem: Check the active ingredient and concentration on your repellent today and pack it in your outdoor bag.

c-069.title: Stainless steel 304 versus 316: reading the label
c-069.summary: For seaside or salty-food use, 316 stainless with molybdenum resists corrosion better.
c-069.principle: Stainless forms a $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ passive film from at least ~10.5% chromium: $\mathrm{4Cr + 3O_2 \to 2Cr_2O_3}$. 316 adds 2-3% molybdenum to resist chloride (Cl−) attack.
c-069.example: 304 (18-8) is fine for ordinary kitchenware but can pit in salty environments. A 316 flask costing 20-30% more lasts longer at the beach.
c-069.actionItem: Find the 304 or 316 marking on the bottom of a stainless item you use today.

c-070.title: Fluoride in toothpaste turns enamel into a tougher crystal
c-070.summary: Fluoride ions convert the hydroxyapatite in enamel into fluorapatite, which resists acid better. Rinsing lightly after brushing keeps more fluoride on the teeth.
c-070.principle: $\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2 + 2F^- \to Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6F_2 + 2OH^-}$. Fluorapatite starts dissolving near pH 4.5, compared with about pH 5.5 for hydroxyapatite.
c-070.example: Use a pea-sized amount of 1000-1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste and rinse just once lightly with water to keep its residual protective effect.
c-070.actionItem: After brushing tonight, rinse only once lightly instead of swishing water several times.

c-071.title: Why aluminum pots darken
c-071.summary: Acidic food left in an aluminum pot darkens it, so store leftovers in another container.
c-071.principle: The $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ film on aluminum dissolves in acid: $\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 6H^+ \to 2Al^{3+} + 3H_2O}$, $\mathrm{2Al + 6H^+ \to 2Al^{3+} + 3H_2}$. Alkaline cleaners also damage it.
c-071.example: Tomato sauce (pH about 4.5) left in an aluminum pot overnight can discolor it and add a metallic taste. Boil 2 tablespoons of citric acid or cream of tartar per liter of water for 10 minutes to remove most of the dullness.
c-071.actionItem: Transfer today's leftover soup or sauce from the pot to a glass or stainless container.

c-072.title: What the yellow underarm stain really is
c-072.summary: The yellow underarm stain on white shirts comes from sweat and aluminum in antiperspirant, and oxygen bleach works on it.
c-072.principle: Sweat proteins and fatty acids combine with aluminum salts into insoluble deposits, and oxygen bleach oxidizes the organics: $\mathrm{H_2O_2 \to H_2O + [O]}$
c-072.example: Mix 1 tablespoon percarbonate with a cup of 40 °C water into a thick paste, leave on the stain for 30 minutes, then wash; most color lifts. Chlorine bleach can actually turn protein stains yellower.
c-072.actionItem: Apply an oxygen bleach paste to the underarms of today's white shirt before washing.

c-073.title: A new-furniture smell signals formaldehyde
c-073.summary: The smell of new furniture or wallpaper is volatile organic compounds (VOCs), so air them out with open windows for days.
c-073.principle: Urea resins in plywood adhesive break down and release formaldehyde, $\mathrm{HCHO}$. Emission rises with temperature and humidity.
c-073.example: For the first 2 weeks after new furniture arrives, ventilate for 30 minutes three times a day and add a bake-out at 25-30 °C; levels drop sharply. The indoor guideline is 0.1 ppm or lower.
c-073.actionItem: Ventilate today with cross-ventilation three times, at least 10 minutes each.

c-074.title: Travel water: boiling versus purification tablets
c-074.summary: Unsafe water can be disinfected by boiling at least 1 minute or with chlorine tablets, killing most pathogens.
c-074.principle: Chlorine tablets form hypochlorous acid in water, which oxidizes microbes: $\mathrm{NaDCC + H_2O \to HOCl + \cdots}$, $\mathrm{HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^-}$
c-074.example: Add 1 tablet to 1 L of clear water and wait 30 minutes (longer for Cryptosporidium). Cloudy water should be strained through cloth first, and above 2,000 m extend boiling to 3 minutes.
c-074.actionItem: Pack a purification tablet or portable filter in your travel bag today.

c-075.title: Fleece wash bags reduce microplastics
c-075.summary: Washing synthetic clothes in a bag in cold water sharply cuts the microfibers they shed.
c-075.principle: Polyester is an ester polymer that does not degrade but fragments by abrasion: $\mathrm{n\,HOOC{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH + n\,HOCH_2CH_2OH \to [-OC{-}C_6H_4{-}COO{-}CH_2CH_2O-]_n + 2n\,H_2O}$
c-075.example: A single fleece jacket wash can release thousands to hundreds of thousands of microfibers. A wash bag or filter catches a fair share and keeps them out of rivers, and a colder wash also saves energy.
c-075.actionItem: Zip up fleece and polyester clothes, put them in a wash bag, and run a cold wash today.

c-076.title: Choose low-self-discharge NiMH rechargeable batteries
c-076.summary: Ordinary NiMH cells lose about 20% of their charge per month even when unused. Low-self-discharge types keep 70-85% after a year, which suits remotes and clocks.
c-076.principle: NiMH reaction: $\mathrm{NiOOH + MH \rightleftharpoons Ni(OH)_2 + M}$. Self-discharge happens as hydrogen slowly shifts between the electrolyte and the electrodes.
c-076.example: One low-self-discharge AA cell (about 2000 mAh) recharged 500 times can replace hundreds of disposable alkaline cells, cutting long-term cost sharply.
c-076.actionItem: Today, if any remote or clock uses disposable batteries, plan to switch it to low-self-discharge rechargeables.

c-077.title: Ballpoint ink stains come out with alcohol, not water
c-077.summary: Ballpoint ink is an oil-based ink with dye dissolved in organic solvent, so water barely moves it. Dabbing with a cloth wet with rubbing alcohol dissolves the dye.
c-077.principle: Similar polarity mixes well. Oil-based dyes dissolve far better in ethanol ($\varepsilon \approx 25$) than in water ($\varepsilon \approx 80$).
c-077.example: Place dry paper towel under the stain and dab from the outside inward with a swab of 70% alcohol; the ink transfers to the towel instead of spreading. Test a small hidden spot first.
c-077.actionItem: Today, if you have a ballpoint mark on fabric or furniture, test alcohol on a hidden spot first.

c-078.title: Wilted vegetables revive after a soak in cold water
c-078.summary: Wilted lettuce and spinach are limp because their cells have lost water. Soaking in cold water for 20-30 minutes lets osmosis refill the cells and restore crispness.
c-078.principle: Water moves into cells when the solute concentration inside is higher than outside. The osmotic pressure $\Pi = iMRT$ builds the turgor that stiffens the leaf.
c-078.example: A handful of lettuce left a day too long gains about 5-10% in weight and regains its crunch after a 30-minute soak. Leaves that are slimy or spoiled do not recover.
c-078.actionItem: Today, soak wilted leafy greens from your fridge in cold water for 30 minutes, then shake them dry.

c-079.title: Dust mite allergens fall only with washing at 60°C or hotter
c-079.summary: Mites and allergen proteins in bedding barely drop with cold-water washes. Water near 60°C denatures the proteins, killing mites and reducing allergens.
c-079.principle: Heat unfolds the tertiary structure of proteins so they lose function (thermal denaturation). Mites usually die within minutes at 55-60°C.
c-079.example: Washing sheets and pillowcases at 60°C cuts allergens substantially, while a 30°C wash helps little. If the care label forbids it, a hot dryer cycle is an alternative.
c-079.actionItem: Today, wash your pillowcases or sheets on the hottest cycle the care label allows.

c-080.title: Camp fuel and winter butane
c-080.summary: Isobutane canisters weaken near freezing, so use propane-blend fuel for late-winter camping.
c-080.principle: Liquefied gases do not vaporize below their boiling points: butane about $-1^\circ\mathrm{C}$, isobutane $-12^\circ\mathrm{C}$, propane $-42^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Combustion: $\mathrm{C_4H_{10} + \tfrac{13}{2}O_2 \to 4CO_2 + 5H_2O}$
c-080.example: Below 0 °C a butane canister loses pressure, the flame weakens, and boiling water can take twice as long. Keep the can warm in a sleeping bag or close to your body, and ventilate in a tent to avoid CO poisoning.
c-080.actionItem: Check the butane/propane ratio on your camp fuel canister today.

c-081.title: Reading sunscreen ingredients
c-081.summary: Before spring UV climbs, learn the difference between mineral (zinc oxide) and chemical filters when you choose.
c-081.principle: Zinc oxide ($\mathrm{ZnO}$) reflects and scatters UV, while organic filters such as avobenzone absorb it and release heat: $h\nu + \text{filter} \to \text{filter}^* \to \text{heat}$
c-081.example: SPF 50 blocks about 98% of UVB and SPF 30 about 97%, a small gap. For the face you need about 0.5 g (two finger lengths) reapplied every 2-3 hours.
c-081.actionItem: Squeeze two finger lengths of sunscreen and apply it before going out today.

c-082.title: Draining food waste cuts both its smell and its weight
c-082.summary: The stench of food waste comes from microbes breaking down protein into gases such as hydrogen sulfide. Squeezing out the water first slows microbial growth, reducing odor and weight.
c-082.principle: Sulfur amino acid breakdown: $\mathrm{R{-}SH \to H_2S}$. Microbial growth slows as water activity $a_w$ drops.
c-082.example: Food waste is 70-80% water. Squeezing out just 20% of that water cuts the weight by roughly 15%, lowering disposal cost and odor together.
c-082.actionItem: Today, drain and squeeze your food waste in a strainer before throwing it out.

c-083.title: Shelf life is set by how reaction rates depend on temperature
c-083.summary: Spoilage reactions roughly double in speed for every 10°C rise. That is why the stated storage temperature must be kept for the date label to mean anything.
c-083.principle: Arrhenius equation: $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$. For typical spoilage reactions the rate rises about 2-3 times per 10°C.
c-083.example: Milk that lasts 7 days at 4°C may spoil in about 3-4 days at 14°C. Store it on an inner shelf rather than the door, where temperature swings more.
c-083.actionItem: Today, check that your refrigerator is between 0 and 4°C.

c-084.title: Washing soda for greasy grime
c-084.summary: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) cuts old kitchen grease better than baking soda because it is more alkaline.
c-084.principle: Fats (triglycerides) saponify in alkali: $\mathrm{RCOOR' + OH^- \to RCOO^- + R'OH}$. Washing soda $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ has a pH of about 11.
c-084.example: Dissolve 1 tablespoon in 1 L of hot water, soak 10 minutes, and wipe to loosen baked-on grease. It irritates skin, so wear gloves, and avoid aluminum and coated pans.
c-084.actionItem: Soak one range hood filter in washing soda solution today.

c-085.title: Fine dust from frying
c-085.summary: Frying and grilling raise indoor PM2.5 sharply, so turn on the hood and open a window while cooking.
c-085.principle: Oil heated beyond about 180 °C thermally decomposes into particles and acrolein: $\mathrm{C_3H_5(OH)_3 \to CH_2{=}CHCHO + 2H_2O}$ (glycerol dehydration)
c-085.example: Measurements show pan-frying mackerel can push indoor PM2.5 to hundreds of μg/m³, and running the hood cuts it considerably. Keep the hood on 10 minutes after cooking.
c-085.actionItem: Turn on the hood before you start cooking today and leave it on 10 minutes after.

c-086.title: Rinse your bike and car after the beach
c-086.summary: Sea salt corrodes metal quickly, so rinse your car and bike with fresh water after a beach trip.
c-086.principle: Sodium chloride solution acts as an electrolyte for iron corrosion cells: $\mathrm{Fe \to Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$, $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \to 4OH^-}$
c-086.example: Iron corrodes several times faster in salty damp air than in dry air. Washing the underbody and chain with water within 24 hours of a coastal drive and oiling the chain greatly cuts rust.
c-086.actionItem: If you went to the coast, rinse your car underbody and bike chain with water today.

c-087.title: Washing produce: water first, baking soda second
c-087.summary: Running water is the basis, and a 12-minute baking soda soak has been reported to remove somewhat more surface pesticide.
c-087.principle: Some pesticides (such as thiabendazole) degrade more easily in mild alkali. A 1% $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ solution has pH about 8.1.
c-087.example: In a study, apples soaked 12 minutes in 1% baking soda (10 g per liter) lost more surface residue than with plain water. Rinse again under running water afterward for fruit you eat with the peel.
c-087.actionItem: Soak apples or grapes in 10 g/L baking soda water today, then rinse.

c-088.title: Bird droppings and bug splatter are protein and need soaking first
c-088.summary: Droppings and insect fluids contain acids and proteins that bake onto paint as they dry. Soaking with a wet cloth first and then wiping gently limits paint damage.
c-088.principle: Dried proteins clump together and hydrogen-bond to the surface. Water and a mild alkaline cleaner (pH 8-9) break these bonds.
c-088.example: Droppings left a day or more can visibly etch paint within 1-2 days, so laying a wet microfiber towel on them for 5 minutes before wiping is safer.
c-088.actionItem: Today, if there is dried bird dropping on your car or window, lay a wet cloth on it for 5 minutes, then wipe it off.

c-089.title: Baking powder and baking soda are different ingredients
c-089.summary: Baking soda is just sodium bicarbonate and needs an acid to rise, while baking powder already contains acid and rises when it meets water. Swapping them can leave a bitter taste or a flat bake.
c-089.principle: $\mathrm{NaHCO_3 + H^+ \to Na^+ + H_2O + CO_2\uparrow}$. One teaspoon of baking soda (about 5 g) can release close to 1 L of carbon dioxide.
c-089.example: If a recipe has 1/2 teaspoon of baking soda plus yogurt (an acid), the acid reacts the soda. Soda alone in a batter without acid leaves unreacted soda with a soapy, bitter taste.
c-089.actionItem: Today, check the labels on your baking soda and baking powder and keep them in separate, labeled containers.

c-090.title: Store apples and bananas apart
c-090.summary: Apples release ethylene, which ripens bananas faster, so keep different fruits apart.
c-090.principle: Ethylene $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2}$ is a plant hormone that activates cell-wall-degrading enzymes and speeds ripening. Its release surges as fruit ripens.
c-090.example: Unripe bananas in a bag with an apple ripen a day or two sooner, which you can use on purpose. To keep bananas longer, store apples separately to gain a day or two and reduce food waste.
c-090.actionItem: Put apples and bananas in separate spots or containers today.

c-091.title: Tannins in tea and coffee block iron absorption
c-091.summary: Tannins and polyphenols in tea and coffee bind iron ions into complexes that are hard to absorb. Leave at least 1-2 hours between them and iron supplements or iron-rich meals.
c-091.principle: Tannins chelate iron: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + tannin \to Fe{-}tannin\ complex}$. This complex is poorly absorbed in the gut.
c-091.example: Tea taken with a meal is reported to cut non-heme iron absorption by 40-60%. Waiting an hour after eating reduces the effect greatly.
c-091.actionItem: If you took iron or ate spinach or beans today, delay tea or coffee by an hour.

c-092.title: Chilling an onion first reduces tears when cutting
c-092.summary: Cutting an onion breaks cells so an enzyme makes a gas that irritates the eyes. Refrigerating the onion for 30 minutes slows that enzyme and reduces tears.
c-092.principle: Alliinase converts sulfoxides into an irritant: propanethial S-oxide ($\mathrm{C_3H_6OS}$) stimulates eye nerves and triggers tears. Enzyme reaction rate falls as temperature drops.
c-092.example: An onion chilled to 4°C for 30 minutes forms the irritant at roughly half the rate or less compared with one at 25°C. Cut the root end last because it holds the most enzyme.
c-092.actionItem: Today, put the onion in the fridge 30 minutes before you cut it.

c-093.title: Wrinkles are hydrogen bonds that have reset in a new shape
c-093.summary: In fibers like cotton, water and heat free the hydrogen bonds between chains, and they set again in a new shape as the fabric cools. Steam and heat release them, and smoothing before it cools removes wrinkles.
c-093.principle: The $\mathrm{{-}OH}$ groups on cellulose chains hydrogen-bond to each other. Moisture and heat break these bonds, and they re-form in the flattened shape as it cools.
c-093.example: Suitable iron temperatures are about 200°C for cotton and below 110°C for synthetics. Hanging clothes in a steamy bathroom after a hot shower can relax light wrinkles on its own.
c-093.actionItem: Check the care label of the shirt you plan to wear today and steam it at the allowed temperature.

c-094.title: Wash fine dust off with a 30-second surfactant cleanse
c-094.summary: Fine dust clings to skin oil, so water alone barely moves it. A foaming cleanse removes oil and dust together.
c-094.principle: Surfactants have an oil-loving tail and a water-loving head; above the critical micelle concentration they trap sebum and dust inside micelles that rinse away. $c>\mathrm{CMC}\;\Rightarrow\;\text{micelle}\ (\text{sebum + dust trapped inside})$
c-094.example: Rubbing a foaming cleanser for 30 seconds in 30-35 °C water removes most surface dust. Skin surface pH is about 4.7-5.5, so a mildly acidic (pH 5-6) cleanser suits it.
c-094.actionItem: After going out today, build a good lather in lukewarm water and cleanse gently for 30 seconds (avoid hot water).

c-095.title: Dry cabin air on a flight calls for moisturizer and water
c-095.summary: Cabin relative humidity is usually 10-20%, desert-like, so skin and nasal membranes lose water quickly. Moisturizer and frequent sips of water help.
c-095.principle: Relative humidity $RH = \dfrac{p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}{p^{*}_{\mathrm{H_2O}}} \times 100\%$. Cabin air is heated outside air, so the saturation pressure is high while the actual vapor pressure is low, giving a low $RH$.
c-095.example: Normal indoor humidity is 40-60%, so water loss in a 10-20% cabin is 2-3 times faster. On a long flight, roughly 100-200 mL of water each hour is a common guideline.
c-095.actionItem: On your next flight, carry moisturizer in a container of 100 mL or less.

c-096.title: Blanch spring greens for just 30 seconds
c-096.summary: A brief blanch stops enzymes, keeps colour vivid and tames bitterness and grassy smell. Long boiling turns chlorophyll dull olive.
c-096.principle: Heat drives air out of the tissue and inactivates colour-degrading enzymes. With heat and acid, magnesium in chlorophyll is replaced by hydrogen ions, giving brownish pheophytin. $\mathrm{Chl\text{-}Mg}+2\,\mathrm{H^+}\rightarrow \mathrm{Pheophytin}+\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$
c-096.example: Blanching 100 g of spinach for 30 s in 1 L of boiling water with 10 g (1%) salt, then chilling it, keeps it bright green; beyond 5 minutes it turns olive.
c-096.actionItem: Next time you buy spring greens, blanch them 30 seconds in 1% salted boiling water and cool them in cold water right away.

c-097.title: Firewood burns best when its moisture is below 20%
c-097.summary: Wet wood spends heat evaporating its water before it burns, giving lots of smoke and little warmth. Wood sheltered from rain and dried for six months or more works best.
c-097.principle: The heat of vaporization of water is $\Delta H_{vap} \approx 2.26\ \mathrm{MJ/kg}$, which is subtracted from the wood's heat of combustion (about $18\ \mathrm{MJ/kg}$ dry basis).
c-097.example: Green wood at 40% moisture delivers about 30% or more less usable heat than dry wood (15-20%) and makes more soot. Split a log to check that its center is dry.
c-097.actionItem: If you will use firewood outdoors, stack it somewhere dry and airy, away from rain.

c-098.title: Brew green tea in 70-80°C water for less bitterness
c-098.summary: Green tea catechins dissolve strongly at high temperatures, making it bitter and astringent, while the savory amino acid theanine comes out well even at lower temperatures. Water cooled to 70-80°C balances them.
c-098.principle: Solubility generally rises with temperature. The catechin epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is extracted quickly above 80°C, increasing astringency.
c-098.example: Tea brewed in 90°C water for 3 minutes extracts noticeably more catechin than tea brewed at 70°C, tasting more bitter. Pouring boiled water into a cup first drops it by about 10°C.
c-098.actionItem: When brewing green tea today, pour the boiled water into a cup first to cool it, then steep for 2 minutes.

c-099.title: Glacial acetic acid is not vinegar; it is 99% acetic acid
c-099.summary: Vinegar is a 4-8% acetic acid solution, while glacial acetic acid is about 99% pure and can burn skin and eyes. For food use it must be labeled food grade and diluted heavily.
c-099.principle: Vinegar: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ about $0.7\ \mathrm{mol/L}$ (4-5%). Glacial acetic acid is about $17\ \mathrm{mol/L}$, more than 20 times stronger. Pure acetic acid freezes into ice-like crystals below 16.6°C, hence the name.
c-099.example: If a recipe uses 5% vinegar, using the same amount of 99% glacial acid adds about 20 times as much acid. Without a food-use dilution on the label, it is safer not to buy it.
c-099.actionItem: Today, check the acidity (%) and ingredients on your household vinegar label.

c-100.title: Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde in the liver, which causes hangovers
c-100.summary: The liver breaks alcohol into acetaldehyde, which causes headaches and nausea until it converts to acetic acid. Drinking water does not speed up the liver's breakdown.
c-100.principle: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{ADH} CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{ALDH} CH_3COOH}$. A typical adult liver clears only about $7\ \mathrm{g}$ of pure alcohol per hour.
c-100.example: Processing a bottle of soju (about 360 mL, roughly 50 g alcohol) takes the liver over 7 hours. Water eases dehydration but does not speed up breakdown.
c-100.actionItem: If you are drinking today, have a glass of water alongside and set a limit beforehand.

c-101.title: A campfire must be put out completely with water
c-101.summary: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat, and removing any one puts it out. Pouring plenty of water over the embers and stirring until the ashes are cold prevents re-ignition.
c-101.principle: Of the three elements of combustion, water removes heat. Water's heat of vaporization $\approx 2.26\ \mathrm{MJ/kg}$ absorbs a great deal of the embers' heat.
c-101.example: A lump of charcoal (about 100 g) gives off several MJ, and 1 L of water can absorb up to about 2.3 MJ by evaporating. Keep pouring until holding the back of your hand near feels no heat.
c-101.actionItem: When you use a fire outdoors, fill a bucket of water beforehand for putting it out.

c-102.title: Sodium on the label x 2.54 = salt
c-102.summary: The sodium figure is the mass of sodium ions, not table salt (sodium chloride). Converting to salt makes your daily intake easier to grasp.
c-102.principle: Dividing the molar mass of NaCl, 58.44 g/mol, by that of Na, 22.99 g/mol, gives about 2.54, so multiply sodium by 2.54 to get salt. $m_{\mathrm{NaCl}}=m_{\mathrm{Na}}\times\frac{58.44}{22.99}\approx 2.54\,m_{\mathrm{Na}}$
c-102.example: A pack of instant noodles with 1,800 mg sodium equals about 4.6 g of salt, nearly all of the WHO guideline of under 5 g salt (2,000 mg sodium) per day.
c-102.actionItem: Today, multiply the sodium mg of one packaged food at home by 2.54 to see its salt in grams.

c-103.title: Pasta can finish cooking on residual heat with the stove off
c-103.summary: After boiling noodles for 2-3 minutes, you can turn off the heat and cover the pot, and the starch keeps cooking. This reduces gas use.
c-103.principle: Starch gelatinization begins around 60-70°C and continues while the water stays above about 90°C. Reaction rate rises with temperature.
c-103.example: In a covered pot, the water drops only about 5-8°C in five minutes after the burner is off, so gelatinization continues. You can save 3-4 minutes of gas.
c-103.actionItem: When boiling pasta or noodles today, turn off the heat after two thirds of the package time and cover the pot.

c-104.title: Keep cut flowers fresh with sugar and a splash of vinegar
c-104.summary: Cut stems still respire and burn sugar. A little sugar and mild acidity feed them and cut the bacteria in the vase.
c-104.principle: Cut flowers use glucose for energy by respiration, and mildly acidic water (about pH 3.5-4) slows bacterial growth that clogs the stem's water channels. $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}+6\,\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow 6\,\mathrm{CO_2}+6\,\mathrm{H_2O}$
c-104.example: Mixing 10 g of sugar (1%) and 5 mL of vinegar into 1 L of water gives about pH 3.7, and changing it every 2 days usually adds several days.
c-104.actionItem: Today, refresh the vase with 1 L of clean water, 10 g of sugar and 5 mL of vinegar, and re-cut the stems at an angle.

c-105.title: Wipe sticker goo away with cooking oil
c-105.summary: Sticky residue left by a label will not wash off with water, but oil dissolves it. You rarely need a harsh solvent.
c-105.principle: Adhesive is a nonpolar polymer, so it resists polar water but mixes with nonpolar oil (like dissolves like). $\delta_{\text{oil}}\approx\delta_{\text{adhesive}}\;\Rightarrow\;\text{like dissolves like}$
c-105.example: Rub a few drops of cooking oil on the residue, wait 5 minutes, wipe, then remove the oil with dish soap; most glass and ceramic labels come clean.
c-105.actionItem: Today, dab oil on a sticky label mark on a jar or plate, wait 5 minutes and wipe it off (acetone can damage plastic).

c-106.title: Nuts go rancid because their unsaturated fats oxidize
c-106.summary: Unsaturated fatty acids in nuts and sesame oil oxidize on contact with air and develop a stale smell. Airtight storage in the freezer delays rancidity by months.
c-106.principle: Lipid autoxidation begins with $\mathrm{RH + O_2 \to ROOH}$ and produces odorous aldehydes. The reaction rate roughly halves with each 10°C drop.
c-106.example: Walnuts at room temperature (25°C) start tasting rancid within weeks to a few months, but airtight at -18°C they keep 6-12 months. Discard nuts that taste bitter or stale.
c-106.actionItem: Today, put leftover nuts in a zip bag or airtight container and store them in the freezer.

c-107.title: Heat can ease the itch of a mosquito bite
c-107.summary: A mosquito's saliva triggers histamine release, causing swelling and itching. Brief heat of about 50°C denatures proteins in the saliva and quiets the itch signal.
c-107.principle: Histamine $\mathrm{C_5H_9N_3}$ stimulates nerve endings, and heat unfolds the saliva proteins' structure to reduce the reaction (thermal denaturation).
c-107.example: Reports suggest about 10 seconds of 50°C heat relieves itching for several hours. To avoid burns, never hold a hot object on skin for long.
c-107.actionItem: On your next trip, pack an anti-itch or cooling gel for mosquito bites.

c-108.title: Potassium sorbate on a label is a mold-inhibiting preservative
c-108.summary: Potassium sorbate inhibits molds and yeasts in acidic foods and is used in cheese, drinks and bread. It is considered safe within regulatory limits, but sensitive people can check for it on labels.
c-108.principle: Sorbic acid ($\mathrm{C_5H_7COOH}$, $pK_a = 4.76$) is more undissociated at low pH, and that form crosses cell membranes to do its work.
c-108.example: At pH 4.8 about 50% of sorbic acid is the active undissociated form, but at pH 6.8 only about 1% is. That is why it works better in acidic foods.
c-108.actionItem: Today, find the preservative listing on the ingredient labels of two foods you often eat.

c-109.title: Spent batteries belong in a collection bin, not general trash
c-109.summary: Batteries contain metals such as zinc, manganese and nickel that can leach into soil if landfilled. A battery collection bin lets those metals be recovered.
c-109.principle: Alkaline cell reaction: $\mathrm{Zn + 2MnO_2 + H_2O \to ZnO + 2MnOOH}$. Recovered, these metals become new raw material.
c-109.example: One AA battery weighs about 23 g, and over 20% of that is metals like zinc and manganese. Collecting 100 batteries (about 2.3 kg) allows a large share of that metal to be recycled.
c-109.actionItem: Today, gather your spent batteries in one container and drop them off at a local collection bin.

c-110.title: Hardened brown sugar softens with a slice of bread
c-110.summary: Brown sugar hardens as moisture leaves the molasses film and the crystals stick together. Sealing it with a slice of bread or damp paper towel returns moisture and softens it.
c-110.principle: Sugar is hygroscopic and draws in water vapor $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$, so the molasses film on its surface softens again. Equilibrium is set between the vapor pressure in the air and at the sugar surface.
c-110.example: Sealing 500 g of hardened brown sugar with one slice of bread usually softens it within a day. In a hurry, covering it with a damp paper towel and microwaving for 20 seconds loosens it.
c-110.actionItem: If you have hardened sugar today, seal it in an airtight container with a slice of bread.

c-111.title: Kelp releases more umami when steeped long in cold water
c-111.summary: Glutamic acid in kelp comes out slowly even in cold water, while hard boiling releases slime that clouds and thickens the broth. Steep in cold water 30 minutes or more, then remove just before boiling.
c-111.principle: Glutamic acid $\mathrm{HOOC{-}CH_2CH_2{-}CH(NH_2){-}COOH}$ is water soluble, while slimy polysaccharides such as alginate dissolve heavily with long boiling.
c-111.example: Two 10 cm strips of kelp in 1 L of water for 30 minutes, removed as the water starts to boil (about 90°C), give plenty of umami. The removed kelp can be reused in braised dishes.
c-111.actionItem: When making broth this evening, soak kelp in cold water for 30 minutes before heating.

c-112.title: Urine color shows whether you are drinking enough
c-112.summary: Urine is yellow because of a pigment called urochrome, and it darkens when water intake is low. Pale yellow generally means you are drinking enough.
c-112.principle: In concentration $c = \dfrac{n}{V}$, less water intake shrinks $V$, so the same amount of urochrome $n$ looks more intense.
c-112.example: About 1.5 L of urine a day in a pale straw color is generally adequate. Dark amber is a cue to drink more, but B vitamins or medications can change the color.
c-112.actionItem: Today, glance at your urine color once and drink a glass of water if it is dark.

c-113.title: Gasoline grades are octane ratings; use the one your car requires
c-113.summary: Octane rating measures how well fuel resists knocking, or self-igniting under compression. If your manual recommends a grade, paying for a higher one gives no benefit.
c-113.principle: Octane number compares knock resistance on a scale where isooctane ($\mathrm{C_8H_{18}}$) is 100 and heptane is 0.
c-113.example: If the manual recommends 91 (regular) and you pump 94 (premium), you pay hundreds of won more per liter for almost no efficiency gain. Use premium only if the engine, such as a high-compression one, requires it.
c-113.actionItem: Today, check the recommended octane in your car manual or on the label inside the fuel door.

c-114.title: Cosmetic ingredient lists are in descending order of amount
c-114.summary: On cosmetic labels, ingredients above 1% are listed from most to least, and those under 1% may be in any order. The first few ingredients make up most of the product, so a headline ingredient near the end is present in small amounts.
c-114.principle: Most products list water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$) first. When concentration $w = \dfrac{m_{\mathrm{ingredient}}}{m_{\mathrm{total}}} \times 100\%$ is below 1%, any order is allowed.
c-114.example: If a toner lists water, glycerin, then butylene glycol, those three can make up over 90% of it. A promoted ingredient listed last is usually under 1%.
c-114.actionItem: Today, read the first five ingredients on one cosmetic you use.

c-115.title: Move camp food quickly through the 4-60°C danger zone
c-115.summary: Bacteria multiply fast between roughly 4 and 60°C, known as the danger zone. Keep meat and egg dishes below 4°C in a cooler and cook them thoroughly to the center.
c-115.principle: Bacterial count grows as $N = N_0 \cdot 2^{t/t_d}$. E. coli can double about every 20 minutes near 37°C.
c-115.example: Food left out at 30°C in midsummer for two hours can see bacteria multiply by about $2^{6} = 64$ times. Cook meat to a core temperature of 75°C or higher for at least a minute.
c-115.actionItem: On your next camping trip, fill the cooler with ice and bring a food thermometer.

c-116.title: Salting pasta water barely raises the boiling point
c-116.summary: Salt does not make the water much hotter. To save gas, use a lid and a lower flame instead.
c-116.principle: Dissolved particles raise the boiling point (boiling-point elevation), but the effect is tiny. $\Delta T_b=i\,K_b\,m=2\times0.512\times0.171\approx0.17\ \mathrm{K}$
c-116.example: Adding 10 g of salt to 1 L of water raises the boiling point only about 0.17 °C, so cooking time is unchanged and you just season the pasta.
c-116.actionItem: Today, salt noodle water only for taste, and once it boils, cover and turn the flame down.

c-117.title: Treat grass stains with alcohol first, then enzyme detergent
c-117.summary: Grass stain mixes oily chlorophyll with protein, so water alone fails. The right order lifts it.
c-117.principle: Chlorophyll dissolves in ethanol, and protease in enzyme detergent cuts protein stains into peptides. Hot water sets protein stains. $\text{protein stain}+\mathrm{H_2O}\xrightarrow{\ \text{protease}\ }\text{peptides}$
c-117.example: Dabbing 70% ethanol on the stain for 5 minutes and then washing at 30-40 °C with enzyme detergent fades most grass stains.
c-117.actionItem: Today, dab a grass stain with disinfectant ethanol for 5 minutes and wash at 30-40 °C (test colourfastness on a hidden spot first).

c-118.title: Eat spinach with lemon to absorb more iron
c-118.summary: Plant (non-haem) iron is poorly absorbed, but vitamin C converts it to an absorbable form. Tannins in tea and coffee do the opposite.
c-118.principle: Non-haem iron is mostly $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, but the gut absorbs $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$; vitamin C reduces ferric to ferrous iron and chelates it. $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}+\text{ascorbate}\rightarrow\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}+\text{dehydroascorbate}$
c-118.example: About 100 mg of vitamin C (roughly one lemon) with a meal can raise non-haem iron absorption about 2-3 times.
c-118.actionItem: Today, squeeze lemon on a spinach or bean dish, and have tea or coffee an hour after the meal.

c-119.title: Chill drinks fast outdoors with salted ice
c-119.summary: Mixing salt into ice drops the temperature far below 0 °C, so drinks cool in minutes. Handy at a picnic.
c-119.principle: Freezing-point depression means salty water freezes only below 0 °C, so melting ice draws heat from its surroundings and the temperature plunges (eutectic -21 °C). $\Delta T_f=i\,K_f\,m,\quad K_f=1.86\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$
c-119.example: Mixing ice and salt 3:1 by mass reaches roughly -15 to -20 °C, and a can spun in it cools to about 5 °C within minutes.
c-119.actionItem: At your next picnic, mix 3 parts ice with 1 part salt in the cooler and roll a can for 3-5 minutes (check it does not freeze and burst).

c-120.title: Brown meat is not automatically spoiled
c-120.summary: Meat colour reflects the state of iron in myoglobin, which does not always match freshness. Judge by date and smell too.
c-120.principle: Oxymyoglobin, bound to oxygen, is bright red; when its iron oxidizes it becomes brown metmyoglobin. Inside vacuum or tight packs there is little oxygen, so meat looks dark purple. $\mathrm{Mb}(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}})+\mathrm{O_2}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{MbO_2}$ (red),  $\mathrm{Mb}\rightarrow\mathrm{metMb}(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}})$ (brown)
c-120.example: Ground beef turns bright red within 15-30 minutes in air and may brown after some days in the fridge, but colour alone is not proof of spoilage.
c-120.actionItem: When shopping for meat today, check the use-by date, the packaging, and any sour smell or sliminess, not only colour.

c-121.title: Let chopped garlic rest 10 minutes before cooking to form allicin
c-121.summary: Cutting or crushing garlic lets the enzyme alliinase convert alliin into allicin, the basis of garlic's antibacterial and health compounds. Heating immediately stops the enzyme so less allicin forms.
c-121.principle: Alliin $\xrightarrow{\text{alliinase}}$ allicin ($\mathrm{C_6H_{10}OS_2}$). The enzyme denatures quickly above about 60-70°C.
c-121.example: Reports suggest that minced garlic rested 10 minutes keeps several times more allicin-derived compounds than garlic cooked right away. One or two cloves per serving is plenty.
c-121.actionItem: If you cook with garlic today, chop it and let it rest 10 minutes before heating.

c-122.title: Strain and shade frying oil to make it last
c-122.summary: Oil goes rancid when exposed to heat, light and oxygen, and smells bad. Storing it well avoids waste.
c-122.principle: Unsaturated fatty acids oxidize by a radical chain reaction, forming peroxides and aldehydes; heat and food particles speed it up. $\mathrm{R}\cdot+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow\mathrm{ROO}\cdot,\ \ \mathrm{ROO}\cdot+\mathrm{RH}\rightarrow\mathrm{ROOH}+\mathrm{R}\cdot$
c-122.example: Use highly unsaturated oils within about 3 months of opening, and reuse strained frying oil only 2-3 times.
c-122.actionItem: Today, strain used frying oil through a coffee filter into a dark bottle and keep it cool; discard it if it smells like paint.

c-123.title: Stainless steel can rust if salty soup sits too long
c-123.summary: Stainless resists rust thanks to a thin chromium-oxide film, but chloride can break it and leave tiny pits and rust spots.
c-123.principle: With over 10.5% chromium a $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ film forms and self-heals in oxygen, but $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ locally destroys it and causes pitting corrosion. $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\ (1\text{-}5\ \mathrm{nm\ film})\ +\ \mathrm{Cl^-}\rightarrow\text{pitting}$
c-123.example: Grade 316, with about 2% molybdenum, resists salt better than 304 (about 18% Cr, 8% Ni). Salt water left for hours can cause pits.
c-123.actionItem: Today, wash any stainless pot that held soup or salty food right away and dry it fully.

c-124.title: Afternoon coffee still lingers at night
c-124.summary: Caffeine leaves the body slowly, so late coffee can disturb night sleep. Moving your last cup earlier helps.
c-124.principle: Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours (range 3-7 h) and declines by a fixed fraction per hour, like a first-order process. $C(t)=C_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/t_{1/2}},\quad t_{1/2}\approx5\ \mathrm{h}$
c-124.example: If you drink 150 mg of caffeine at 3 pm, about 50 mg (one third) remains 8 hours later at 11 pm. A daily total up to 400 mg is the usual guideline.
c-124.actionItem: Today, set your last caffeinated drink at least 8 hours before bedtime and switch to decaf or barley tea afterwards.

c-125.title: At altitude water boils near 95 °C, so cooking slows
c-125.summary: Air pressure falls with height, so water boils at a lower temperature. That is why instant noodles and rice come out undercooked.
c-125.principle: Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point (about 3.3 °C per 1,000 m). With the rule that rates double per 10 °C, cooking time lengthens. $\Delta T_b\approx -3.3\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\ \text{per}\ 1000\ \mathrm{m};\quad \frac{t'}{t}\approx 2^{\Delta T/10}$
c-125.example: At 1,500 m water boils near 95 °C, so the rate is $2^{-0.5}\approx0.7$ of normal and cooking takes about 40% longer.
c-125.actionItem: If you are hiking today, plan 1.4 times the usual time for instant noodles and cook rice longer with a lid on.

c-126.title: Never preheat a non-stick pan empty on high heat
c-126.summary: PTFE (Teflon) coatings are stable to about 260 °C but break down above that and give off harmful fumes. Preheating an empty pan on high is the most common home cause.
c-126.principle: PTFE is stable thanks to very strong C-F bonds, but above roughly 300 °C it decomposes and releases fluorinated gases that are deadly to pet birds. $-(\mathrm{CF_2\text{-}CF_2})_n-,\quad E_{\mathrm{C\text{-}F}}\approx485\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$
c-126.example: An empty pan on high heat can pass 300 °C within 2-5 minutes, while cooking with oil or food on medium heat usually stays under 200 °C.
c-126.actionItem: Today, use non-stick pans on medium or lower heat with oil or food in them, never empty, and skip metal utensils.

c-127.title: Drinking undiluted vinegar dissolves tooth enamel
c-127.summary: Vinegar's pH is about 2.5, far below the pH 5.5 at which enamel begins to dissolve. If you drink it, dilute it well and rinse with water afterward.
c-127.principle: Enamel dissolution: $\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2 + 14H^+ \to 10Ca^{2+} + 6H_2PO_4^- + 2H_2O}$. The lower $\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^+}]$, the faster it dissolves.
c-127.example: Vinegar at pH 2.5 has 1000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of pH 5.5. Mix one tablespoon into at least 200 mL of water, drink it through a straw, and brush 30 minutes later.
c-127.actionItem: If you drink vinegar or a sour drink today, rinse with water and wait 30 minutes before brushing.

c-128.title: Freeze bread, do not refrigerate it
c-128.summary: Bread goes hard not by drying but because starch recrystallizes, and that happens fastest in the fridge.
c-128.principle: Starch retrogradation, where amylose and amylopectin realign into crystals, is fastest at 0-5 °C and nearly stops below -18 °C. $\text{amylose/amylopectin recrystallization (retrogradation)},\ \text{fastest at }0\text{-}5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$
c-128.example: Room-temperature bread keeps 2-3 days and fridge bread stales faster, whereas bread at -18 °C keeps about 3 months, and heating above 60 °C melts the crystals and softens it.
c-128.actionItem: Today, slice leftover bread, freeze it in portions, and reheat in a toaster or steamer when needed.

c-129.title: Fix tomato stains in plastic containers with oil and sunlight
c-129.summary: The red pigment in tomato sauce mixes with oil and soaks into plastic. Oil and UV light work better than water.
c-129.principle: Lycopene is a nonpolar pigment that dissolves into plastic; its 11 conjugated double bonds absorb light and look red, and UV breaks them into colourless fragments. $\text{lycopene (11 conjugated C=C)}\xrightarrow{h\nu}\text{colourless fragments}$
c-129.example: Rub on a drop of oil, wash with dish soap, then leave the container in sunlight for 2-3 hours; most of the stain fades.
c-129.actionItem: Today, rub a drop of cooking oil on a stained plastic box, wash it with soap, and set it on a sunny windowsill for 2-3 hours (glass containers prevent it).

c-130.title: Oral rehydration uses salt and sugar together
c-130.summary: When glucose and sodium are absorbed together, water follows. It rehydrates better than plain water.
c-130.principle: The SGLT1 transporter in gut cells carries one glucose with two sodium ions, and water is drawn in by osmosis. $\mathrm{SGLT1}:\ 1\ \text{glucose}+2\ \mathrm{Na^+}\rightarrow\text{water uptake}$
c-130.example: The WHO home recipe is 1 L of boiled-and-cooled water with 6 level teaspoons (about 25 g) of sugar and half a teaspoon (about 3 g) of salt. Severe dehydration, infants or high fever need medical care.
c-130.actionItem: Today, stock a packet or two of commercial oral rehydration salts (ORS) in your medicine box.

c-131.title: Stinging pool eyes are chloramines, not chlorine itself
c-131.summary: Red eyes do not mean the pool is over-chlorinated; they come from chloramines formed when chlorine meets sweat and urine. A pre-swim shower is the best prevention.
c-131.principle: Chlorine becomes hypochlorous acid (HOCl) in water and disinfects; with ammonia-type nitrogen it forms irritating chloramines. At pH 7.5 about 50% is HOCl. $\mathrm{Cl_2}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{HOCl}+\mathrm{H^+}+\mathrm{Cl^-},\quad \mathrm{HOCl}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{H^+}+\mathrm{OCl^-}\ (\mathrm{p}K_a\approx7.5)$
c-131.example: Recommended pool values are pH 7.2-7.8 and free chlorine 1-3 ppm. A 1-minute soap shower before swimming greatly cuts organic load.
c-131.actionItem: Before going swimming today, take a 1-minute soapy shower, and do not urinate in the pool.

c-132.title: Compute water hardness from the mineral-water label
c-132.summary: Bottled waters differ in hardness, which changes how coffee and tea taste and how much scale you get. The label numbers are enough to tell soft from hard.
c-132.principle: Hardness expresses calcium and magnesium ions as an equivalent mass of calcium carbonate. About 50-175 mg/L is recommended for brewing coffee. $H=2.497\,[\mathrm{Ca}]+4.118\,[\mathrm{Mg}]\ (\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}\text{ as }\mathrm{CaCO_3})$
c-132.example: Water with 80 mg/L calcium and 26 mg/L magnesium is $2.497\times80+4.118\times26\approx307$ mg/L, very hard (above 180), and will scale a kettle quickly.
c-132.actionItem: Today, calculate the hardness of the bottled water you drink from the Ca and Mg numbers on its label.

c-133.title: Calories are heat of combustion: 4-4-9 kcal per gram
c-133.summary: Food energy is defined by the heat released when food is burned. You can work out calories yourself from the grams on a label.
c-133.principle: Burning 1 mol of glucose releases 2,803 kJ (about 15.6 kJ/g, 3.7 kcal/g). Atwater factors are 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat. $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}+6\,\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow6\,\mathrm{CO_2}+6\,\mathrm{H_2O},\ \Delta H=-2803\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\approx3.7\ \mathrm{kcal\,g^{-1}}$
c-133.example: A snack with 50 g carbohydrate, 20 g fat and 10 g protein gives $50\times4+20\times9+10\times4=420$ kcal.
c-133.actionItem: Today, use the nutrition label of one snack to calculate its kcal from the grams of carbs, fat and protein.

c-134.title: Drying laundry in sunlight also bleaches it
c-134.summary: Ultraviolet light breaks down leftover pigment stains in fabric, making whites look brighter. Small stains fade in sunlight even without percarbonate.
c-134.principle: Photo-oxidation: UV photons break the $\pi$ bonds in pigments, which react with oxygen to form colorless products. Photon energy $E = h\nu$ must exceed the bond energy.
c-134.example: A stained white T-shirt hung wet in direct sun for 4-6 hours fades light stains noticeably. Colored clothes can fade by the same principle, so dry them inside out.
c-134.actionItem: Today, hang a stained white garment wet in a sunny spot to dry.

c-135.title: Soak superglued fingers in soapy water
c-135.summary: Superglue cures on skin moisture, but warm soapy water can loosen it slowly. Pulling apart tears skin.
c-135.principle: Cyanoacrylate polymerizes by chain reaction when moisture (OH⁻) triggers it, hardening in seconds to a minute. Soapy water and gentle rubbing soften and push off the bond. $n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(CN)COOR}\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{OH^-}\ (\text{moisture})\ }\left[\mathrm{CH_2\text{-}C(CN)(COOR)}\right]_n$
c-135.example: Soaking in warm soapy water for 10-15 minutes and rolling with a thumb frees most fingers. If it sticks to eyes or lips, do not rub; get medical care.
c-135.actionItem: Today, ventilate when using superglue, and if fingers stick, soak them in warm soapy water for 15 minutes and roll them apart.

c-136.title: Adding acid reduces fishy smell
c-136.summary: The main culprit in fishy odor is trimethylamine, a basic compound. Sprinkling lemon juice or vinegar neutralizes it so less smell escapes.
c-136.principle: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N + H^+ \to (CH_3)_3NH^+}$. The ionized amine does not evaporate, so the odor falls.
c-136.example: A teaspoon (about 5 mL) of lemon juice on a fish fillet for 5 minutes noticeably reduces the fishy smell. Soaking in milk for 20 minutes works on a similar principle, with proteins binding the odor compounds.
c-136.actionItem: When cooking fish today, first splash it with lemon juice or vinegar.

c-137.title: Oxygen partial pressure drops with altitude and makes you breathless
c-137.summary: The oxygen fraction in air is about 21% everywhere, but air pressure falls with altitude, so oxygen partial pressure drops. At 3000 m you take in only about 70% as much as at sea level.
c-137.principle: Dalton's law: $p_{\mathrm{O_2}} = x_{\mathrm{O_2}} \times P_{\mathrm{total}}$. $x_{\mathrm{O_2}} \approx 0.21$ stays constant while $P_{\mathrm{total}}$ falls.
c-137.example: At sea level (101 kPa) oxygen partial pressure is about 21 kPa, and at 3000 m (about 70 kPa) it is about 14.7 kPa. Ascending slowly, within about 500 m per day, lowers altitude sickness risk.
c-137.actionItem: If you plan a high-altitude trip, schedule a gradual ascent.

c-138.title: Discard cans that bulge or are badly dented
c-138.summary: A bulging can signals that microbes inside produced gas, possibly dangerous bacteria such as Clostridium botulinum. Do not open bulging cans; throw them away.
c-138.principle: Microbial fermentation gas: reactions such as $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \to 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2}$ produce $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and raise the pressure inside the can.
c-138.example: A normal can is near vacuum inside, so its lid is flat or slightly concave. If it bulges, hisses loudly or foams on opening, do not eat it.
c-138.actionItem: Today, check the cans in your pantry for bulging or rust.

c-139.title: Grease poured down a sink drain cools, hardens and clogs it
c-139.summary: Hot oil is liquid, but as it cools its saturated fats solidify on pipe walls and bind with debris. Wipe oil off with paper and put it in the trash, not the drain.
c-139.principle: Saturated fats melt around 30-60°C, and cooling oil goes through a $\mathrm{liquid \to solid}$ phase change. With calcium ions it also forms fatty acid calcium salts (soap scum).
c-139.example: Pouring 200 mL of frying oil down the drain can leave a 1-2 mm hardened layer on pipe walls, and repeating it can clog the pipe. Wipe greasy dishes with paper towel before washing.
c-139.actionItem: Today, wipe greasy pans with paper towel before washing them.

c-140.title: Water bottles left in a hot car
c-140.summary: PET bottles left in a hot car can release more trace antimony and other compounds. A day or two is low risk, but water left for weeks is best avoided.
c-140.principle: Leaching rises with temperature: $k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$ (Arrhenius equation, larger $T$ gives larger $k$)
c-140.example: A midsummer car interior can reach 60-70 °C, making leaching several times faster than at 20 °C.
c-140.actionItem: Do not drink PET-bottle water that has sat in your car; carry a stainless-steel tumbler for trips instead.

c-141.title: Why the R-32 refrigerant matters
c-141.summary: R-32 needs less charge than R-410A for the same cooling capacity and has roughly one third of the global warming potential (GWP). It is worth checking when you buy an air conditioner.
c-141.principle: R-32 is $\mathrm{CH_2F_2}$; a large latent heat $q = h_{\mathrm{g}} - h_{\mathrm{f}}$ means less refrigerant must circulate.
c-141.example: GWP is about 2088 for R-410A and about 675 for R-32. The charge is also about 20-30% smaller, giving slightly higher efficiency.
c-141.actionItem: When you buy or service an AC, read the label and note the refrigerant type (R-32 or R-410A).

c-142.title: Why soda goes flat
c-142.summary: Carbon dioxide dissolves best under pressure and in the cold, and escapes when the drink warms or the pressure drops. Keep it cold and recap quickly.
c-142.principle: Henry's law: $C = k_{\mathrm{H}}\,P_{\mathrm{CO_2}}$, where $k_{\mathrm{H}}$ falls as temperature rises.
c-142.example: Pressure in a sealed bottle is about 3-4 atm, and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ solubility at 25 °C is roughly half that at 4 °C.
c-142.actionItem: Recap the soda right after pouring and store it upright in the fridge today.

c-143.title: Baking soda in the fridge
c-143.summary: Baking soda is mildly basic, so it neutralises acidic odour molecules such as fatty acids. Its capacity is small, so replace it every 2-3 months.
c-143.example: About 100 g (half a cup) in an open container is enough to tame mild odours in a small fridge.
c-143.actionItem: Put a cup of baking soda in a shallow dish on a fridge shelf and write a replacement date 3 months out.

c-144.title: Sweet potatoes taste sweetest when baked slowly through 70-75°C
c-144.summary: Beta-amylase in sweet potato breaks starch into sweet maltose, working best around 70-75°C and stopping above 90°C. The slower the bake, the longer it spends in the sweet zone.
c-144.principle: $\mathrm{(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n + n/2\,H_2O \xrightarrow{\beta\text{-amylase}} n/2\,C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}$. Enzyme activity has an optimum temperature.
c-144.example: Baking at 150°C or below for 50 minutes or more keeps the interior in the 70-75°C range much longer than 5 minutes at 180°C, producing far more maltose. That is why roasted sweet potatoes are so sweet.
c-144.actionItem: When baking sweet potatoes today, roast them low and slow.

c-145.title: Eggs turn soft-boiled around 62-65°C because proteins denature
c-145.summary: Egg white and yolk proteins set at different temperatures. The white begins to set at about 62-65°C and the yolk at about 65-70°C, which separates soft-boiled from hard-boiled.
c-145.principle: Thermal denaturation unfolds the tertiary structure of proteins so they tangle together. Ovotransferrin denatures near 62°C and ovalbumin near 80°C.
c-145.example: Six minutes in boiling water gives a set white and runny yolk, while 10 minutes or more gives a hard-boiled egg. Because of Salmonella risk, older adults and pregnant people should eat them fully cooked.
c-145.actionItem: When boiling eggs today, set timers for 6 and 10 minutes and compare the results.

c-146.title: Water-soluble vitamins in excess leave in the urine
c-146.summary: Vitamin C and the B vitamins dissolve in water, so what exceeds your need is not stored but excreted in urine. Much of a high-dose supplement may simply be wasted.
c-146.principle: Water-soluble molecules are polar, dissolve readily in blood and urine, and are filtered by the kidneys. Fat-soluble vitamins, by contrast, accumulate in fat tissue.
c-146.example: The adult vitamin C recommendation is about 100 mg a day, and taking 1000 mg at once drops absorption below 50%, with much of the rest excreted. One fruit supplies about 50 mg.
c-146.actionItem: If you take a vitamin supplement today, check that it plus your food stays within the recommended intake.

c-147.title: Sea salt and refined salt differ in NaCl share and minerals
c-147.summary: Refined salt is 99% or more sodium chloride (NaCl), while solar sea salt is about 80-90% NaCl mixed with magnesium, calcium and moisture. Either way sodium is similar, so eating less matters most.
c-147.principle: The sodium fraction is $\dfrac{M_{\mathrm{Na}}}{M_{\mathrm{NaCl}}} = \dfrac{23}{58.5} \approx 0.39$. For the same salt mass, the higher the NaCl share, the more sodium.
c-147.example: 5 g of pure NaCl holds about 1.97 g of sodium, while sea salt at 85% NaCl holds about 1.67 g. WHO advises under 5 g of salt a day.
c-147.actionItem: Today, check the sodium content (mg per 100 g) on your salt's nutrition label.

c-148.title: Photochromic lenses explained
c-148.summary: Silver halide in photochromic lenses splits into silver specks under UV and darkens, then recombines when the light fades. In cars, glass blocks UV so they darken less.
c-148.example: In sunlight, transmission can fall from about 85% to the 20% range within a minute and recover over 5-15 minutes indoors.
c-148.actionItem: For sunny drives, carry regular UV-blocking sunglasses instead of relying on photochromic lenses.

c-149.title: Electric cars waste less energy than gasoline cars
c-149.summary: A gasoline engine turns only about 20-30% of fuel energy into motion and wastes the rest as heat. An electric car delivers about 80-90% of its electric energy to the wheels, so it needs less energy per distance.
c-149.principle: One liter of gasoline carries about $32\ \mathrm{MJ}$ ($\approx 8.9\ \mathrm{kWh}$), and at efficiency $\eta = \dfrac{W_{\text{out}}}{E_{\text{in}}}$ of about 25% the useful work is roughly 2.2 kWh.
c-149.example: A car that goes about 12 km per liter of gasoline uses that 2.2 kWh of useful work for 12 km, while an electric car covers 12 km on about 2 kWh (roughly 6 km per kWh). Counting power-plant losses narrows the gap.
c-149.actionItem: Today, walk or take transit for short trips to save fuel.

c-150.title: Cooking oil smoke points
c-150.summary: Past its smoke point, oil produces smoke and acrolein that irritate eyes and throat. High-heat cooking calls for oils with a high smoke point.
c-150.example: Smoke points are about 190 °C for extra-virgin olive oil, about 240 °C for canola and about 230 °C for refined sunflower oil.
c-150.actionItem: Use a refined, high-smoke-point oil for stir-frying; if it smokes, lower the heat and ventilate.

c-151.title: Why iced tea turns cloudy
c-151.summary: When strong black tea cools, caffeine and tannins bind into particles and make it cloudy. Adding hot water clears it, and cold brewing avoids it.
c-151.principle: Caffeine + tannin (theaflavin) $\rightleftharpoons$ complex: solubility drops at low temperature, so it precipitates.
c-151.example: Black tea brewed at 100 °C and cooled to 4 °C turns hazy within minutes; cold brew (4 °C, 8 hours) is much clearer.
c-151.actionItem: Make today's iced tea by steeping a tea bag in 500 mL cold water in the fridge for 8 hours.

c-152.title: Amygdalin in plum seeds is dangerous raw
c-152.summary: Unripe green plums and their seeds contain amygdalin, which can release hydrogen cyanide when broken down. Remove the pit or age plum syrup six months or more, strain it, and do not eat the seeds.
c-152.principle: $\mathrm{C_{20}H_{27}NO_{11} + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{enzyme}} C_6H_5CHO + HCN + 2C_6H_{12}O_6}$. Hydrogen cyanide forms when the enzyme contacts it.
c-152.example: The amygdalin in a single plum seed is tiny, but chewing many raw seeds could be dangerous. Layer pitted green plums with sugar at 1:1, age six months, then remove the fruit.
c-152.actionItem: If you make plum syrup today, do not eat the seeds and note on the calendar when to remove the fruit.

c-153.title: Spray cans can burst if left somewhere hot
c-153.summary: Aerosol cans hold compressed gas and a flammable propellant, so pressure rises with temperature. Left in a summer car or near a flame they can burst, so follow the label's storage limit of 50°C or lower.
c-153.principle: Gas pressure is proportional to temperature: $\dfrac{P_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2}{T_2}$ ($T$ in kelvin). The vapor pressure of a liquefied propellant climbs steeply with temperature.
c-153.example: A can at 5 atm at 20°C (293 K) reaches about 5.7 atm at 60°C (333 K) by simple calculation, and far higher once the propellant's vapor pressure is added. A midsummer car interior can exceed 60°C.
c-153.actionItem: Today, gather the spray products at home and move them to a cool spot away from heat.

c-154.title: Why jelly will not set with fresh pineapple or kiwi
c-154.summary: Protein-digesting enzymes in raw pineapple and kiwi chop up gelatin. Heating them once or using canned fruit stops the enzymes so the jelly sets.
c-154.principle: Bromelain and actinidin hydrolyze peptide bonds: $\mathrm{R{-}CO{-}NH{-}R' + H_2O \to R{-}COOH + H_2N{-}R'}$. The enzymes denature above about $70\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
c-154.example: 100 mL of gelatin with raw pineapple stays liquid even after hours, but pineapple heated above 80°C for a minute, or canned pineapple, sets normally. The same enzymes are used to tenderize meat.
c-154.actionItem: When adding fresh fruit to jelly or pudding today, blanch pineapple or kiwi in boiling water for a minute first.

c-155.title: The musty smell of damp towels
c-155.summary: The smell of slow-drying laundry comes from fatty acids such as 4-methyl-3-hexenoic acid produced by Moraxella bacteria. Drying fast before they multiply is the key.
c-155.principle: Bacterial metabolism: skin lipids $\rightarrow$ $\mathrm{C_7H_{12}O_2}$ (4-methyl-3-hexenoic acid) and other volatile fatty acids
c-155.example: If wet laundry stays damp for over 5 hours indoors, odour starts; a dryer at 60 °C or above greatly reduces bacteria.
c-155.actionItem: Hang laundry right after washing and run a fan or dehumidifier so it dries within 5 hours.

c-156.title: What the pink bathroom slime is
c-156.summary: The pink slime is not mould but a red-pigmented film made by bacteria such as Serratia. Moisture and soap residue feed it, so drying is the best prevention.
c-156.principle: Bacterial growth $N = N_0\,2^{t/t_d}$ (a doubling time $t_d$ of 30 min gives hundreds of thousands of times in a day)
c-156.example: In a warm, damp bathroom at 25-35 °C, counts can grow about 4,000-fold every 6 hours; drying stops growth.
c-156.actionItem: After showering, squeegee walls and floor and run the exhaust fan for 30 minutes.

c-157.title: Storing cut watermelon
c-157.summary: A cut watermelon loses water and sugar through its cut face and invites bacteria. Cover the cut surface and refrigerate it, and eat within two days.
c-157.principle: Evaporation scales with exposed area and temperature. At 4 °C, bacterial growth is about 1/20 of that at 25 °C.
c-157.example: At 30 °C a cut melon can have tens of times more bacteria after 2 hours; in the fridge at 4 °C it stays safe about 2 days.
c-157.actionItem: Keep leftover melon in large pieces with the rind on and wrap the cut face tightly before chilling.

c-158.title: Summer lunchboxes are safer with vinegared rice and cooled side dishes
c-158.summary: In acidic conditions (pH below 4.6) most food-poisoning bacteria struggle to grow. Adding a spoon of vinegar to the rice or packing cooled side dishes extends safety.
c-158.principle: With the weak-acid equilibrium $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+}$, a higher $[\mathrm{H^+}]$ lowers pH and slows bacterial growth.
c-158.example: Adding 1 tablespoon (15 mL) of vinegar to 2 cups of rice (about 300 g) lowers its pH to around 5 and slows bacterial growth. Close the lunchbox only after the food has cooled fully, and pack an ice pack.
c-158.actionItem: For today's lunchbox, cool the food fully before closing it and add an ice pack.

c-159.title: Why tools rust on humid days
c-159.summary: Iron forms rust when water and oxygen are present, and it speeds up above about 60% humidity. A thin oil film or desiccant slows it.
c-159.example: At 60%+ relative humidity bare iron can rust within days, but below 40% it barely progresses.
c-159.actionItem: Wipe tools with a lightly oiled cloth and put silica gel in the toolbox.

c-160.title: Mothball safety
c-160.summary: Mothballs go straight from solid to gas (sublimation) to repel insects. The vapour is harmful to breathe, so ventilation and distance matter.
c-160.principle: Sublimation: $\mathrm{C_{10}H_8(s) \rightarrow C_{10}H_8(g)}$; vapour pressure rises with temperature.
c-160.example: Naphthalene vapour pressure is about 11 Pa at 25 °C and roughly 4 times higher at 40 °C. Keep it from touching clothes.
c-160.actionItem: Air clothes stored with mothballs on a balcony for 2-3 hours before wearing, and keep mothballs away from children.

c-161.title: Rubbing hands on stainless steel eases garlic and fish smells
c-161.summary: The sulfur compounds from garlic and onion are said to fade when you rub your hands on stainless steel. Soap helps by washing off and oxidizing the sulfur compounds.
c-161.principle: Sulfur compounds $\mathrm{R{-}SH}$ adsorb onto the oxide film ($\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$) on metal surfaces and become less volatile.
c-161.example: Many people find that rubbing hands on a stainless faucet for 30 seconds after mincing garlic reduces the smell, though scientific evidence for the effect size is limited. Lemon juice or vinegar can also be used.
c-161.actionItem: After mincing garlic today, rub your hands on a stainless sink for 30 seconds and then wash them with soap.

c-162.title: Why bread moulds fast in the rainy season
c-162.summary: Bread has a high water activity, so mould grows quickly above 70% humidity. Its threads reach deep inside, so cutting off only the visible spot is unsafe.
c-162.principle: Water activity $a_w = \dfrac{p}{p_0}$ (bread about 0.95; mould grows above about 0.80)
c-162.example: On a humid day at 25 °C bread moulds in 3-4 days, while frozen at -18 °C it keeps for weeks.
c-162.actionItem: Freeze slices you cannot finish today, wrapped individually, and toast them straight from frozen.

c-163.title: Why rain is slightly acidic
c-163.summary: Rain is mildly acidic at about pH 5.6 because atmospheric CO2 dissolves in it; acid rain is below 5.6. It is harmless to skin at this level but slowly corrodes metal and stone.
c-163.example: $[\mathrm{H^+}] \approx 2.5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ gives pH $= -\log[\mathrm{H^+}] \approx 5.6$, versus 7 for pure water.
c-163.actionItem: After rain, wipe the water off your bicycle chain and add a drop of oil.

c-164.title: Cooled rice gains resistant starch, so less sugar is absorbed
c-164.summary: As rice cools, some of its starch turns into resistant starch that is hard to digest. Even after reheating, some remains, which may soften the blood sugar rise slightly.
c-164.principle: Starch retrogradation is the re-crystallization of gelatinized amylose as it cools. The amylase enzyme breaks these crystals down poorly.
c-164.example: Rice reheated after 12-24 hours in the fridge is reported to have several times more resistant starch than fresh rice, though the increase is only a few percent of total starch. Do not leave rice at room temperature; refrigerate it quickly.
c-164.actionItem: Today, refrigerate leftover rice within one hour.

c-165.title: Fabric softener and towel absorbency
c-165.summary: Fabric softener coats fibres with cationic surfactants, making them soft but less absorbent. For towels, use it less often or skip it.
c-165.principle: Cationic surfactant $\mathrm{R_2N^+(CH_3)_2}$ adsorbs onto negatively charged fibre $\mathrm{{-}COO^-}$ and forms a water-repelling film.
c-165.example: Softener can cut towel absorbency by about 20-30%. Use it in only 1 of every 3 towel loads.
c-165.actionItem: Wash today's towels without softener and shake them out well before drying.

c-166.title: Recycling an aluminum can takes only about 5% of the energy of making a new one
c-166.summary: Making aluminum from ore uses enormous electricity, but recycling it saves about 95%. Rinsing cans and sorting them properly boosts the benefit.
c-166.principle: Electrolysis of bauxite: $\mathrm{2Al_2O_3 \to 4Al + 3O_2}$. New aluminum takes about $14\ \mathrm{kWh}$ per kg, while recycled aluminum takes about $0.7\ \mathrm{kWh}$.
c-166.example: Recycling one aluminum can (about 14 g) saves roughly 0.2 kWh. A hundred cans save about 20 kWh, comparable to running an air conditioner for around five hours.
c-166.actionItem: Today, empty and rinse any cans you drank and put them in the aluminum recycling bin.

c-167.title: Cutting off the visible mold does not make moldy food safe
c-167.summary: Mold sends thread-like hyphae below what you can see, and some molds produce toxins. For soft foods like bread, fruit and jam, it is safest to discard the whole item if mold shows.
c-167.principle: Aflatoxin $\mathrm{B_1}$ ($\mathrm{C_{17}H_{12}O_6}$) is heat stable and decomposes only above about $270\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so boiling or baking does not remove it.
c-167.example: For dense foods like hard cheese or carrots, guidelines say cutting at least 2.5 cm around the moldy spot works, but soft, moist foods such as bread, jam and tofu must be discarded entirely.
c-167.actionItem: Today, check the bread and jam in your fridge for mold.

c-168.title: The smell of city gas is something deliberately added
c-168.summary: City gas (methane) is naturally odorless, so a small amount of rotten-egg-smelling thioether or mercaptan compounds is added to reveal leaks. If you smell it, do not use flames or electric switches; ventilate first.
c-168.principle: Methane is explosive at roughly 5-15% in air: $\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \to CO_2 + 2H_2O}$. Odorants added to odorless gas include compounds such as $\mathrm{CH_3SH}$.
c-168.example: In an 8 m³ space, 0.4-1.2 m³ of leaked methane (5-15%) is within the explosive range. If you smell gas, close the valve, open windows, avoid touching light or fan switches, and report it from outside.
c-168.actionItem: Today, learn where your gas valve is and make a habit of closing it after use.

c-169.title: Optical brighteners in white-laundry detergent make whites look whiter
c-169.summary: Optical brighteners absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as blue light, masking yellow tones so fabric looks whiter. It is a visual effect, not soil removal, and colored clothes do not need it.
c-169.principle: Fluorescence absorbs UV (about 350 nm) and emits blue light (about 430 nm); the emitted photon energy $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ is slightly lower.
c-169.example: A white T-shirt washed with brighteners can look about 5-10% brighter in sunlight because it emits extra blue light. For colored clothes, a regular detergent without them is enough.
c-169.actionItem: On laundry day, check the detergent labels for optical brighteners and use them only on whites.

c-170.title: Putting a wet phone in rice barely helps
c-170.summary: Rice absorbs moisture poorly, so it pulls water out of a phone at about the same rate as air drying. Power it off, do not charge it, and let it dry in a ventilated spot instead.
c-170.principle: Drying rate is proportional to the vapor pressure difference. Rice's desiccating power is far weaker than silica gel, and what matters is how long corrosion can proceed after a short circuit.
c-170.example: Silica gel can absorb up to about 40% of its weight in water, but rice absorbs far less. Keep the phone off for 24-48 hours or more before turning it on. If it fell in salt water, contact a service center first.
c-170.actionItem: If your phone gets wet, skip the rice and power it off and leave it somewhere ventilated.

c-171.title: For a burn, cool it under running water for 20 minutes first
c-171.summary: Immediately after a burn, running cool water (15-25°C) for 10-20 minutes draws out heat that spreads into deeper skin and limits damage. Do not use ice, toothpaste or soybean paste.
c-171.principle: Heat from a hot object transfers to tissue as $q = mc\Delta T$ and denatures proteins. Running water carries heat away quickly.
c-171.example: Water at 60°C can cause a serious burn in 5 seconds. Twenty minutes of cool water reduces burn depth and pain, while very cold ice constricts blood vessels and can further harm tissue.
c-171.actionItem: Remember today: if you burn yourself in the kitchen, cool it under running water for 20 minutes right away.

c-172.title: What oxygen absorbers do in food packs
c-172.summary: The small sachet in seaweed or jerky packs contains iron powder that reacts with oxygen and removes it. Less oxygen slows fat oxidation and mould.
c-172.example: One sachet (about 2 g iron) absorbs about 200 mL of oxygen, nearly removing the 21% in a 1 L pack.
c-172.actionItem: Do not eat the sachet; leave it in the pack until you open it.

c-173.title: Egg freshness float test
c-173.summary: An eggshell has tiny pores, so over time water and CO2 escape and the air cell grows. A fresh egg sinks and an old one floats.
c-173.principle: Buoyancy $F_{\mathrm{b}} = \rho_{\mathrm{water}}\,V g$; once the air cell lowers average density to $\rho < \rho_{\mathrm{water}}$, it floats.
c-173.example: A fresh egg is about 1.09 g/mL; after 3-4 weeks it drops to about 1.02 g/mL and begins to float in plain water.
c-173.actionItem: Before cracking a doubtful egg, drop it in a bowl of water, and discard it if it floats.

c-174.title: Why honey crystallises
c-174.summary: When glucose in honey exceeds what the water can hold, it forms crystals. It is normal, not spoilage, and gentle warming reverses it.
c-174.example: Honey is about 31% glucose, 38% fructose and 17% water, and crystallises faster below 14 °C; a 40 °C water bath dissolves it.
c-174.actionItem: Soak the crystallised jar in water below 40 °C instead of microwaving it.

c-175.title: Why oils and supplements come in brown bottles
c-175.summary: Light, especially UV and blue light, oxidises fats and vitamins and spoils them. Amber glass strongly blocks light below about 450 nm.
c-175.principle: Photo-oxidation: $\mathrm{RH + O_2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} \mathrm{ROO\cdot}$ (chain oxidation); photon energy $E = hc/\lambda$
c-175.example: Amber glass blocks over 90% of light near 400 nm, whereas oil in clear bottles can turn rancid within weeks in sunlight.
c-175.actionItem: Store sesame and perilla oil in a dark cupboard, not on a sunny windowsill.

c-176.title: How instant cold packs get cold
c-176.summary: When ammonium nitrate or urea in the pack dissolves in water it absorbs heat and the temperature drops. Squeeze, shake and it works immediately.
c-176.example: One mole (80 g) of ammonium nitrate absorbs 25.7 kJ on dissolving, cooling 100 mL of water by about 15-20 °C below room temperature.
c-176.actionItem: Pack an instant cold pack for camping or sport, wrap it in a towel and use it for 15 minutes only.

c-177.title: Why lithium-ion batteries hate heat
c-177.summary: High temperature speeds electrolyte breakdown and SEI growth, permanently cutting capacity. Never leave a phone or power bank in a car in midsummer.
c-177.principle: Ageing rate $k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$: roughly 2x faster for each 10 °C rise (Arrhenius rule of thumb)
c-177.example: If a cell loses about 20% capacity in a year at 25 °C, it may lose about 35-40% in the same time at 45 °C.
c-177.actionItem: In summer, never leave battery devices in the car; carry them in your bag.

c-178.title: Why kimchi sours fast in summer
c-178.summary: Lactic acid bacteria in kimchi multiply faster when warm and make more lactic acid. Below 10 °C it ripens slowly and tastes good longer.
c-178.example: At 20 °C pH drops to about 4.2 in 3-4 days and the kimchi turns sour, whereas at 4 °C it changes slowly over weeks.
c-178.actionItem: Portion only what you will eat into a small tub and keep the rest in the coldest part of the fridge.

c-179.title: Sunscreen is oily, so washing with water alone does not remove it
c-179.summary: Sunscreen's UV filters and oils barely dissolve in water, so water alone leaves them behind. Dissolving them with a cleansing oil or balm and finishing with a foaming cleanser removes them well.
c-179.principle: Like dissolves like: similar polarity mixes. Nonpolar oils dissolve in nonpolar cleansers, while water needs surfactant micelles to carry them away.
c-179.example: Water-resistant sunscreens are designed to retain 80% or more after immersion in water. Massaging with cleansing oil for 30 seconds, adding water to emulsify and rinsing is effective.
c-179.actionItem: If you wore sunscreen today, use an oil cleanser first and then a foaming cleanser.

c-180.title: The white crust from a leaking battery is alkaline; wear gloves to clean it
c-180.summary: The white powder from an aged alkaline battery is potassium carbonate, formed when leaked potassium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide in air. It irritates skin and eyes, so wear gloves and wipe it with a swab dampened with vinegar or lemon juice.
c-180.principle: $\mathrm{2KOH + CO_2 \to K_2CO_3 + H_2O}$ forms the white crystals, and a weak acid like vinegar neutralizes it: $\mathrm{K_2CO_3 + 2CH_3COOH \to 2CH_3COOK + H_2O + CO_2}$.
c-180.example: Leaked electrolyte is strongly alkaline at pH 13-14 and irritates bare skin. Wipe with a vinegar-dampened swab and finish with a dry cloth. Taking batteries out of devices you rarely use is safer.
c-180.actionItem: Today, remove the batteries from any remote or toy you do not use for long periods.

c-181.title: Why ice cubes are cloudy
c-181.summary: Dissolved air and impurities get pushed to the middle as water freezes, trapped as a white core. Boiled and cooled water is clearer but not fully transparent.
c-181.principle: Gas solubility $C = k_{\mathrm{H}}\,P$: it drops to almost zero in ice, so bubbles get trapped
c-181.example: Ice made from boiled-and-cooled water has fewer bubbles and is visibly clearer; freezing from one side (directional freezing) gives clear ice.
c-181.actionItem: Fill an ice tray with boiled and cooled water and freeze it for today's drinks.

c-182.title: Storing hydrogen peroxide
c-182.summary: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes into oxygen and water when exposed to light, heat or metals. Keep it cool in a brown bottle; old bottles lose strength.
c-182.example: 3% hydrogen peroxide can lose much of its strength about 6 months after opening, and decomposes faster above 30 °C.
c-182.actionItem: Write the opening date on your hydrogen peroxide bottle and keep it somewhere dark and cool.

c-183.title: Drinking Only Plain Water After Heavy Sweating Can Dilute Blood Sodium
c-183.summary: After sweating for hours, gulping large amounts of plain water can dilute blood sodium and cause headache or nausea. Pair fluids with something salty.
c-183.principle: Sweat removes Na$^+$ along with water. Refilling with plain water only enlarges the denominator in $C_{\mathrm{Na}}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{Na}}}{V}$, so concentration falls and water moves into cells by osmosis. The normal range is about 135-145 mmol/L.
c-183.example: On a 3-hour summer hike you may lose about 2 L of sweat, roughly 2 g of sodium (about 5 g of salt). Drinking 3 L of plain water at once on top of that can push blood Na$^+$ below 135 mmol/L.
c-183.actionItem: During long exercise or walks today, bring a salty snack (nuts, crackers) or a diluted sports drink with your water, and avoid drinking more than 500 mL in one go.

c-184.title: Bleach Mixed in Hot Water Just Loses Its Disinfecting Power
c-184.summary: Mixing bleach into hot water breaks down the active ingredient quickly and mostly adds a harsh chlorine smell. Dilute it in cold or lukewarm water and use it right away.
c-184.principle: The active species HOCl from sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) is heat-sensitive and decomposes as $2\mathrm{HOCl}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{O_2}$. Each roughly 10 °C rise typically speeds decomposition by 2x or more.
c-184.example: A small dose of household bleach (about 4-5% NaOCl) in 500 mL of water stays effective for hours at 20 °C, but in 60 °C water a large share is gone within minutes and more irritating fumes escape.
c-184.actionItem: When disinfecting today, dilute bleach in cold water, use it right away, ventilate the room, and never mix it with acidic cleaners.

c-185.title: Heat Seaside Oysters and Clams to 85 °C for 1 Minute to Stop Vibrio
c-185.summary: Cooking oysters and clams to 85 °C or higher at the core for at least 1 minute greatly reduces Vibrio risk. Raw shellfish is especially risky for people with weak immunity.
c-185.principle: Heat denatures Vibrio proteins so the cells stop functioning. Counts fall as $N=N_0\,10^{-t/D}$, and higher temperatures shorten $D$, the time for a 10-fold reduction.
