c-185.example: Vibrio multiplies fast in 25-35 °C seawater. Cooking 3-5 minutes after the shells open and holding the core at 85 °C for 1 minute adds a good safety margin.
c-185.actionItem: If you eat seafood today, choose fully cooked shellfish over raw, and wash knives and boards that touched raw shellfish right away.

c-186.title: Lime or Lemon Juice on Skin Plus Sun Can Cause Blisters
c-186.summary: Citrus juice left on skin in sunlight can cause burn-like redness and blisters. If juice gets on you, wash with soap and stay out of the sun.
c-186.principle: Furocoumarins in citrus peel and juice absorb UVA (320-400 nm) and bind skin DNA and proteins in a phototoxic reaction. Photon energy is $E=h\nu=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$, higher at shorter wavelength.
c-186.example: If you squeeze limes at an outdoor party and don't wash your hands before 1-2 hours in the sun, red marks and blisters in the shape of the juice can appear 24-72 hours later, with pigmentation lasting months.
c-186.actionItem: If you handle citrus today, wash your hands with soap and water right away, and cover any sun-exposed skin until you have washed.

c-187.title: For a Jellyfish Sting, Rinse With Seawater, Not Fresh Water
c-187.summary: Rinsing a jellyfish sting with fresh water can make leftover stingers fire. Rinse with seawater and remove tentacles with a tool, not bare hands.
c-187.principle: Jellyfish nematocysts fire in response to osmotic and chemical triggers. Fresh water has far lower osmotic pressure than seawater (about 35 g/L salt); by $\Pi=iMRT$ water can rush into the capsules and prompt discharge.
c-187.example: If stung at the beach, rinse with seawater for 30+ seconds, scrape tentacles off with a card edge, and for severe pain a soak in roughly 45 °C water for about 20 minutes is commonly advised. First aid varies by species, so call emergency services for breathing trouble.
c-187.actionItem: If you go to the sea today, check jellyfish warnings and carry a bottle for seawater rinses and a credit card for scraping.

c-188.title: Why Swimsuits Sag After the Pool and How to Pick One
c-188.summary: Swimsuits go baggy after a few pool visits because chlorine breaks down stretch fibers. Choose chlorine-resistant fabric and rinse right after use.
c-188.principle: Spandex (polyurethane) chains are oxidized and cut by HOCl in pool disinfectant. Shorter chains mean less elasticity, and ordinary spandex degrades much faster than chlorine-resistant PBT-based swimwear fabric.
c-188.example: A regular nylon/spandex suit shows clear sagging after 30-50 pool sessions, while PBT blends last several times longer. Pool residual chlorine is typically 1-3 mg/L.
c-188.actionItem: After swimming today, rinse your suit in cold water right away, don't wring it, and dry it in the shade.

c-189.title: Why Re-Frozen Ice Cream Turns Gritty
c-189.summary: When ice cream melts and refreezes, large coarse ice crystals form and make it gritty. After one thaw, it is better to eat it than to refreeze it.
c-189.principle: Small ice crystals have high surface energy, melt, and their water moves onto larger crystals that grow (Ostwald ripening). Solubility rises as radius $r$ shrinks: $\ln\frac{S_r}{S_\infty}=\frac{2\gamma V_m}{rRT}$.
c-189.example: Well-made ice cream has ice crystals under about 50 μm and feels smooth, but after thawing and refreezing they can grow past 100 μm and feel gritty. Freezer temperature swings cause the same effect.
c-189.actionItem: Today, keep ice cream at the back of the freezer instead of the door to limit temperature swings, and close the lid right after serving.

c-190.title: Never Leave Dry Ice in a Closed Car
c-190.summary: Dry ice does not melt but turns into gas, which can raise CO$_2$ in a closed car to dangerous levels. Transport it with windows open or in a ventilated space.
c-190.principle: Solid CO$_2$ sublimes: $\mathrm{CO_2(s)}\rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ (at -78.5 °C). 1 kg makes about 500 L of gas, and CO$_2$ above 4% causes headache and dizziness, with higher levels being dangerous.
c-190.example: 2 kg of dry ice releases about 1,000 L of CO$_2$. If it fully evaporates in a car cabin of about 3,000 L, the concentration could climb to about 25%, which is very dangerous.
c-190.actionItem: If you carry dry ice today, keep the space ventilated, handle it with gloves, and never put it in a sealed container.

c-191.title: Corn Loses Its Sweetness the Longer It Sits After Picking
c-191.summary: From the moment corn is picked, its sugars turn into starch and the sweetness fades. Boil it the day you buy it or refrigerate it to keep sweetness longer.
c-191.principle: Enzymes in the kernels convert sugars such as glucose into starch: $n\,\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\rightarrow(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}O_5})_n+n\,\mathrm{H_2O}$. Enzyme reactions slow in the cold, so refrigeration delays the change.
c-191.example: Fresh sweet corn left at room temperature for a day can convert about 40% of its sugar to starch, while at 0-4 °C refrigeration the process is much slower. Keeping the husk on also reduces moisture loss.
c-191.actionItem: If you bought corn today, refrigerate it in its husk instead of leaving it out, and cook it within a day if you can.

c-192.title: Why Refrigerating Tomatoes Kills Their Flavor
c-192.summary: Chilling a ripe tomato dulls its aroma and makes the texture mealy. Keep ripe tomatoes at room temperature and eat them within a few days.
c-192.principle: Below about 12 °C tomatoes suffer chilling injury, which lowers the activity of enzymes that make aroma compounds (such as cis-3-hexenal) and damages membranes. Enzyme rate depends on temperature via $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$.
c-192.example: Just 3 days in a 5 °C fridge can sharply cut a tomato's volatile aroma compounds. At room temperature, ripe tomatoes are best eaten within about 3-5 days.
c-192.actionItem: Today, store ripe tomatoes stem-side down in a cool spot, and if already chilled, take them out 30 minutes before eating.

c-193.title: How to Rescue Broken Mayonnaise
c-193.summary: Don't throw out mayonnaise whose oil and egg have separated. Whisk it little by little into a fresh egg yolk to bring it back; the fresh yolk's lecithin re-establishes the emulsion.
c-193.principle: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil dispersed in water, and lecithin in the yolk lowers the oil-water interfacial tension $\gamma$ so droplets don't merge. If oil goes in too fast or temperatures are off, droplets coalesce and the phases separate.
c-193.example: About 200 g of broken mayonnaise can be smoothed again by whisking it spoonful by spoonful into 1 new yolk and 1 teaspoon of water. One yolk can typically emulsify up to about 200 mL of oil.
c-193.actionItem: If you make mayonnaise today, start adding oil drop by drop, then slowly speed up, use fresh eggs, and refrigerate it after making.

c-194.title: Menthol Cooling Products Don't Actually Lower Body Temperature
c-194.summary: Menthol cooling sprays and sheets only make you feel cool; they don't really lower body temperature. Water and shade come first for heat relief.
c-194.principle: Menthol activates the cold receptor TRPM8 in skin, sending your nerves a cold signal. Real heat transfer needs a temperature change, as in $Q=mc\Delta T$, and menthol itself removes almost no body heat.
c-194.example: A cooling product with about 1% menthol changes skin temperature by roughly 0.5 °C at most, yet the cool feeling lasts tens of minutes. In heatwaves above 33 °C, trusting the sensation alone is risky.
c-194.actionItem: On a hot day today, don't rely on cooling products alone; drink water and rest in the shade to actually lower your temperature.

c-195.title: For a Burning Mouth, Take a Sip of Milk Instead of Water
c-195.summary: When spicy food makes your mouth burn, water does little but milk or yogurt works better. Capsaicin clings to fats and proteins.
c-195.principle: Capsaicin ($\mathrm{C_{18}H_{27}NO_3}$) is a fat-soluble molecule that barely dissolves in water. Milk fat dissolves it and casein protein binds it, helping lift it off receptors.
c-195.example: After spicy noodles, 200 mL of water only rinses briefly, while a cup of milk (200 mL, about 7 g fat, about 6 g protein) noticeably calms the burn within minutes.
c-195.actionItem: With spicy food today, have milk or plain yogurt alongside, and if your mouth is on fire, hold a sip in your mouth before swallowing.

c-196.title: The Charred Parts of Charcoal-Grilled Meat Contain Benzo[a]pyrene
c-196.summary: Blackened, charred bits of meat grilled over open charcoal can contain benzo[a]pyrene, a probable carcinogen. Trim charred parts and keep flames from touching the meat.
c-196.principle: When meat fat drips onto coals and pyrolyzes, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) form and rise in smoke to coat the meat. A key one is benzo[a]pyrene ($\mathrm{C_{20}H_{12}}$).
c-196.example: Grilling fatty pork belly directly over flames raises benzo[a]pyrene in smoke and char. Wiping the grill often and using foil or a plate instead of a grate can cut PAHs substantially.
c-196.actionItem: If you grill meat today, use moderate heat away from dripping-fat flare-ups, and cut off any blackened parts before eating.

c-197.title: Use Graphite Powder, Not Oil, in a Key Lock
c-197.summary: For a sticky key lock, graphite powder (pencil lead dust) works better than ordinary oil. Oil attracts dust and makes the lock stickier over time.
c-197.principle: Graphite is a solid lubricant whose carbon layers slide over each other. It lowers the friction coefficient $\mu$ in $F=\mu N$ and, being dry, doesn't collect dust.
c-197.example: A puff or two of graphite powder in the keyhole reduces friction so the key turns smoothly. Ordinary oil mixes with dust and can gum up within months, clogging the lock.
c-197.actionItem: If a key is stiff today, puff a little graphite lubricant into the keyhole, or rub pencil lead onto the key's grooves and slide it in and out a few times.

c-198.title: Use Chain Oil, Not WD-40, on a Bicycle Chain
c-198.summary: WD-40 is mostly a solvent and cleaner and doesn't last as a bicycle chain lubricant. After cleaning, apply oil made for chains.
c-198.principle: WD-40 is volatile solvent with a thin oil film that evaporates or washes off fast. A lubricant's higher viscosity keeps a film between contact surfaces, cutting friction loss $P_{\mathrm{loss}}=F_f\,v$.
c-198.example: A clean, well-lubricated chain is about 98-99% efficient, while a dry, dirty one can lose 3 percentage points or more. At 150 W of pedaling, 3% is about 4.5 W lost.
c-198.actionItem: If your chain squeaks today, wipe it with a dry cloth, put one drop of chain oil on each link, then wipe off the excess.

c-199.title: When Aluminum Touches Stainless Steel, One Corrodes First
c-199.summary: When dissimilar metals touch in moisture, the more active one corrodes first. When bolting aluminum to stainless steel, put an insulating washer between them.
c-199.principle: Two metals with different potentials plus an electrolyte form a small cell, and aluminum dissolves at the anode: $\mathrm{Al}\rightarrow \mathrm{Al^{3+}}+3e^-$. Standard potentials differ a lot: about -1.66 V for Al versus roughly -0.44 V or higher for stainless (Fe-based).
c-199.example: On a seaside terrace, using stainless screws directly in an aluminum railing can produce white powdery corrosion at the contact in months to a year, because the potential gap is large and seawater is a good electrolyte.
c-199.actionItem: Today, check places where different metals touch, and where water collects, separate them with an insulating washer or paint.

c-200.title: Don't Put Food in a Galvanized Bucket
c-200.summary: Putting acidic food (vinegar, pickled fruit, kimchi) in a zinc-galvanized bucket or sheet can leach zinc and cause vomiting and stomach pain. Use food-grade containers.
c-200.principle: The zinc coating dissolves in acid: $\mathrm{Zn}+2\mathrm{H^+}\rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}+\mathrm{H_2}$. Acidic foods have pH 4 or lower, so the reaction is fast.
c-200.example: At a campsite, lemonade or pickles at about pH 3 left in a galvanized bucket for hours can pick up tens of mg/L of zinc, risking vomiting and nausea. The adult daily recommended intake is only about 8-11 mg.
c-200.actionItem: When camping or cooking outdoors today, use only containers marked food-safe, and keep galvanized buckets for hauling water.

c-201.title: Check Imported Ceramic Cups for Lead Leaching From the Glaze
c-201.summary: Shiny imported ceramic cups can leach lead from the glaze into acidic drinks. Look for food-safe labels and test results, and don't leave acidic drinks in them long.
c-201.principle: Lead compounds in glaze dissolve in acid: $\mathrm{PbO}+2\mathrm{H^+}\rightarrow \mathrm{Pb^{2+}}+\mathrm{H_2O}$. Leaching rises with lower pH, such as vinegar or fruit juice, and with longer contact.
c-201.example: In the test of soaking in 4% acetic acid for 24 hours, Korea's limit for cups is 0.4 mg/L of lead. Decorative ceramics without a test report may exceed this limit.
c-201.actionItem: Today, check imported ceramic cups for a food-safe mark and test report, and don't fill unverified decorative cups with acidic drinks such as juice or wine.

c-202.title: Perfume Left in a Car Changes Its Scent
c-202.summary: Perfume left in a hot car changes smell and loses its freshness. Store it in a cool, dark place.
c-202.principle: Light top-note molecules are highly volatile and evaporate faster as temperature rises. Vapor pressure grows exponentially with temperature, $\ln P=-\frac{\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}}}{RT}+C$, and heat, light and oxygen oxidize fragrance components.
c-202.example: A parked car in midsummer can exceed 60 °C inside, evaporating perfume several times faster than a 20 °C room. After a few weeks, citrus top notes fade and the liquid can darken.
c-202.actionItem: Today, move perfume from the car or bathroom to a cool, dark drawer and close the cap tightly after use.

c-203.title: Ointments and Creams Left in a Summer Car Can Separate
c-203.summary: Ointments and creams left in a hot car can separate into water and oil and change, reducing effectiveness. Store medicines at the temperature on the label (usually 30 °C or below).
c-203.principle: A cream is an emulsion of water and oil stabilized by emulsifiers. Heat lowers emulsifier performance and viscosity so droplets merge and phases separate. Reaction rates are temperature-sensitive, $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$.
c-203.example: A parked car in midsummer can exceed 60 °C, so a cream can thin out or release oil within hours. Once separated, a product may not return to its original state even when remixed.
c-203.actionItem: When you go out today, carry ointments, sunscreen and medicines in your bag rather than leaving them in the car.

c-204.title: Camping Alcohol Stoves: Methanol and Ethanol Are Not the Same
c-204.summary: For camping alcohol stoves, methanol is toxic and burns with a nearly invisible flame, so denatured ethanol is the safer choice. Check whether it's lit, and put the flame out before refueling.
c-204.principle: Ethanol burns as $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}+3\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO_2}+3\mathrm{H_2O}$ and methanol as $2\mathrm{CH_3OH}+3\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO_2}+4\mathrm{H_2O}$. A methanol flame is almost transparent, and the body metabolizes it to formic acid, making it highly toxic.
c-204.example: Ethanol releases about 27 kJ/g when burned versus about 20 kJ/g for methanol, so ethanol gives more heat per gram. A small swallowed amount of methanol can cause blindness and poisoning.
c-204.actionItem: When using an alcohol stove today, check the fuel type, and refuel only after the flame is out and the stove has cooled.

c-205.title: Don't Keep Mower or Trimmer Gasoline Longer Than About Three Months
c-205.summary: Gasoline stored over about three months for a brush cutter or generator degrades, causing hard starts and clogged carburetors. Buy only what you need, or use fuel stabilizer for leftovers.
c-205.principle: Light fractions of gasoline evaporate and oxidation forms sticky gum that clogs fuel lines. Ethanol blends absorb water and can phase-separate. Oxidation proceeds as $\mathrm{RH}+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow$ peroxides and other products.
c-205.example: In a sealed can, regular gasoline typically starts having problems after 3-6 months and ethanol blends after 1-3 months. A full, cool container lasts longer because less air contacts the fuel.
c-205.actionItem: If you won't use your brush cutter for long, empty the fuel or add stabilizer today, and keep leftover fuel in a sealed, cool place.

c-206.title: If You Put Gasoline in a Diesel Car, Don't Start the Engine
c-206.summary: If you mistakenly put gasoline in a diesel car, don't start it and call a tow. The fuel pump and injectors can be damaged.
c-206.principle: Diesel engines use compression ignition (air compressed to high heat self-ignites the fuel), but gasoline resists ignition and has low viscosity, so it doesn't lubricate. Diesel compression ratio is about $\varepsilon=15\sim 20$.
c-206.example: Gasoline mixing in weakens lubrication of the high-pressure pump and can cause metal wear, with repairs costing millions of KRW (thousands of USD). Draining the tank without starting the engine usually prevents damage.
c-206.actionItem: When refueling today, check the pump handle color and fuel type, and if you filled the wrong fuel, don't turn the key and call a repair shop.

c-207.title: AdBlue Diesel Exhaust Fluid Degrades in Summer Heat
c-207.summary: If kept hot for long, the urea in diesel exhaust fluid breaks down, its concentration drops, and it smells of ammonia. Store it in a cool shaded place and don't use old fluid.
c-207.principle: The fluid (32.5% urea solution) hydrolyzes to ammonia, $\mathrm{(NH_2)_2CO}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}+\mathrm{CO_2}$, and in the SCR unit reduces nitrogen oxides, $4\mathrm{NH_3}+4\mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow 4\mathrm{N_2}+6\mathrm{H_2O}$.
c-207.example: Stored at 25 °C or below it typically lasts about a year, but above 30 °C that shrinks to a few months, and in a 50 °C car trunk quality can fall within weeks. The concentration drifts from the 32.5% spec.
c-207.actionItem: Today, keep exhaust fluid in a cool spot out of direct sun, and check any bottle left long in the trunk before using it.

c-208.title: Judge Engine Oil by Oxidation and Additive Depletion, Not Just Mileage
c-208.summary: When to change engine oil depends on time, short trips and hot weather as well as mileage. Use the maker's interval as a baseline and shorten it under severe conditions.
c-208.principle: Engine oil oxidizes at high temperature, thickening and forming sludge, while additives such as detergents and dispersants are used up and trap acids and soot less well. Oxidation follows $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, roughly doubling for each 10 °C rise.
c-208.example: If the maker recommends 10,000 km or 1 year, severe use such as only short trips or driving in heatwaves calls for a change at about 5,000-7,500 km or 6 months. Even at 5,000 km a year, change it after a year.
c-208.actionItem: Today, check the service sticker or manual for the change interval and compare it to your last oil-change date.

c-209.title: Is Filling Tires With Nitrogen Worth It?
c-209.summary: Nitrogen-filled tires lose pressure a bit more slowly, but the effect is small. What matters most is checking pressure once a month, not the gas type.
c-209.principle: Rubber lets oxygen through about 3-4 times faster than nitrogen. Air is about 78% N$_2$ and 21% O$_2$, so nitrogen fill reduces O$_2$ permeation and slows the pressure drop. At fixed volume, pressure follows $P=\frac{nRT}{V}$, proportional to moles and temperature.
c-209.example: Air-filled tires typically lose about 1-2 psi (about 7-14 kPa) a month, and nitrogen only somewhat less. A 10 °C drop in air temperature reduces pressure by about 1 psi in both nitrogen and air.
c-209.actionItem: Today, check tire pressure when the tires are cold and set it to the spec printed on the door-jamb label.

c-210.title: A Lunchbox Left at Room Temperature Keeps Its Toxins Even if Reheated
c-210.summary: Lunchboxes or rice rolls left out in summer can carry toxins that reheating or boiling won't remove once they start to spoil. If in doubt, throw it out.
c-210.principle: Enterotoxins made by Staphylococcus aureus growing at room temperature are heat-stable, and most remain even after 30+ minutes at 100 °C. The bacteria die but the toxin protein structure isn't easily destroyed, so symptoms still occur.
c-210.example: Bacteria multiply fast at 20-37 °C and can make toxin within hours, with vomiting and stomach pain starting 1-6 hours after eating. Food left out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 30 °C) after cooking is risky.
c-210.actionItem: Today, pack lunch in a cooler bag with an ice pack, and throw away food left at room temperature more than 2 hours after cooking.

c-211.title: Don't Wash Dishes With Detergent in a Stream or the Sea
c-211.summary: Washing dishes with detergent in a stream or at the beach pollutes water, can kill fish and cause algal blooms. Wash up only in designated campground areas.
c-211.principle: Surfactants in detergent damage aquatic organisms' gill membranes, and phosphates add nutrients that cause algal blooms and eutrophication. When algae die, decomposition uses oxygen and lowers dissolved oxygen (DO).
c-211.example: Even one drop of ordinary dish detergent (about 0.05 mL) can affect aquatic life in tens of liters of water. When stream dissolved oxygen falls below 5 mg/L, fish struggle to survive.
c-211.actionItem: Outdoors today, carry food scraps out with you and wash dishes at the campground's designated greywater point.

c-212.title: Mosquitoes Follow Your Breath and Sweat Odor
c-212.summary: Mosquitoes follow the carbon dioxide you exhale and the lactic acid smell in sweat to find where to bite. Wiping sweat and applying repellent lowers your chance of bites.
c-212.principle: Receptors on mosquito antennae track concentration gradients, moving toward higher CO$_2$ and lactic acid ($\mathrm{C_3H_6O_3}$). Exhaled air is about 4% CO$_2$, about 100 times the roughly 0.04% in ambient air.
c-212.example: A person exhales about 1 kg of CO$_2$ a day, and after exercise sweat lactic acid rises, so mosquitoes can find you from tens of meters away. DEET 10-30% products typically protect for several hours.
c-212.actionItem: Before going outdoors today, wipe off sweat, apply repellent to exposed skin and clothing, and empty any standing water.

c-213.title: Sewer Smell From a Floor Drain Rises When the Trap Seal Dries Out
c-213.summary: If a drain smells like sewage, its trap water seal has probably dried out. Pour a jug of water down to refill the seal and block the odor.
c-213.principle: Water held in the trap's U-bend (the seal) blocks sewer gas. When it evaporates, hydrogen sulfide ($\mathrm{H_2S}$) made by microbes in the sewage can rise. Seal depth is commonly about 50 mm.
c-213.example: An unused bathroom floor drain's seal can dry within 1-2 weeks, letting odor through. Pouring about 500 mL of water refills it, and in summer evaporation is faster so it dries more often.
c-213.actionItem: Today, pour a jug of water into unused bathroom or balcony drains to refill the seal, and repeat once a month.

c-214.title: Why Air Conditioners Smell Sour
c-214.summary: A sour smell from an air conditioner comes from bacteria and mold growing in condensed water and dust inside. Drying the inside with fan mode before turning off helps.
c-214.principle: Water condenses on the cooling fins as $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\rightarrow \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, and microbes grow in dust and organic matter, producing volatile metabolites (fatty acids, alcohols, etc.) that smell sour.
c-214.example: Turning off right after cooling leaves internal humidity above 80%, so bacteria grow easily. Running fan mode for 10-30 minutes before shutting off dries most of the interior and cuts the smell sharply.
c-214.actionItem: Today, run the AC in fan mode for 15 minutes before turning it off, and remove the filter to dust it off and let it dry.

c-215.title: White Film on Chocolate Isn't Mold
c-215.summary: The white film on chocolate is usually not mold but fat bloom, cocoa butter that melted and resolidified. The texture gets slightly coarse but it is safe to eat.
c-215.principle: Cocoa butter has several crystal forms (polymorphs). The stable form V converts to the more stable form VI with temperature changes and rises to the surface, appearing white. Form V melts at about 34 °C.
c-215.example: Stored above 28 °C or with frequent temperature swings, bloom can appear in days to weeks. The best chocolate storage is about 15-18 °C at 50% relative humidity or lower.
c-215.actionItem: Today, keep chocolate in a cool spot out of direct sun, and when taking it from the fridge, leave it in its wrapper at room temperature to prevent condensation.

c-216.title: Mackerel and Tuna Left at Room Temperature Form Histamine
c-216.summary: Red-fleshed fish such as mackerel and tuna can form histamine if left out, causing facial flushing, headache and hives. Cooking doesn't remove it, so keep fish fresh and cold.
c-216.principle: Bacterial histidine decarboxylase converts the fish's histidine to histamine: $\mathrm{C_6H_9N_3O_2}\rightarrow \mathrm{C_5H_9N_3}+\mathrm{CO_2}$. Histamine is heat-stable and hardly destroyed by cooking.
c-216.example: Histamine can form within hours at 25 °C but far more slowly at 4 °C. Food limits are typically 200 mg/kg or less, and eating 100 mg or more may cause symptoms.
c-216.actionItem: Today, refrigerate or freeze red-fleshed fish as soon as you bring it home, and don't eat fish left at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

c-217.title: Why Old Tents and Rain Gear Turn Sticky
c-217.summary: The waterproof coating inside an old tent or rain jacket becomes sticky and peels because polyurethane hydrolyzes in moisture and heat. Storing it fully dry slows this down.
c-217.principle: Ester bonds in polyurethane (PU) coating react with water and break, $\mathrm{R{-}COO{-}R'}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightarrow \mathrm{R{-}COOH}+\mathrm{R'{-}OH}$, shortening the chains so the coating turns tacky. Hot, humid conditions speed it up.
c-217.example: PU-coated tents typically begin to hydrolyze after 3-5 years. Folded damp and stored above 30 °C, they can turn sticky within a single season.
c-217.actionItem: Today, dry tents and rain gear completely, then store them unfolded in a cool place, and if already sticky, consider replacing rather than recoating.

c-218.title: Why Laundry Capsules Stay as Clumps
c-218.summary: Laundry capsules stay clumped when the water is cold, too little, or the load is too full. Put the capsule in the bottom of the drum first, then add clothes on top.
c-218.principle: The PVA (polyvinyl alcohol) film around a capsule dissolves in water, and the dissolving rate depends strongly on temperature, slowing at low temperature as with $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, so it doesn't dissolve well in cold water.
c-218.example: PVA film dissolves in about 1-3 minutes in 40 °C water but can take over 10 minutes in cold water at 15 °C or below. A drum stuffed with laundry presses the capsule against fabric so water can't reach it.
c-218.actionItem: Today, don't touch capsules with wet hands, put them in the drum first and clothes over them, and use liquid detergent for cold-water cycles.

c-219.title: Camping Glow Sticks Shine Through a Chemical Reaction
c-219.summary: A camping glow stick lights up when you bend it and two liquids inside mix in a chemical reaction. It shines without electricity or heat, brighter and shorter when warm, dimmer and longer when cold.
c-219.principle: Hydrogen peroxide and an oxalate ester inside the tube react to form a high-energy intermediate, which excites a fluorescent dye so it emits light (chemiluminescence). The rate is temperature-sensitive, $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$.
c-219.example: A glow stick typically lasts 6-12 hours at 20 °C, but at 40 °C it is much brighter and can fade in 1-2 hours, while in a freezer it dims and brightens again when warmed. It gives off almost no heat, so fire risk is low.
c-219.actionItem: For night camping or a power outage today, tuck one or two glow sticks into your bag, and keep any leaked liquid off your skin.

c-220.title: Fireworks Colors Come From Metal Elements' Flame Emission
c-220.summary: Firework colors come from metal elements mixed into the powder. Strontium gives red, copper gives blue, and barium gives green.
c-220.principle: The flame's heat excites electrons in metal atoms, and when they fall back to lower energy levels they emit light of energy $E=h\nu=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$. Each element has different levels, so each has its own color.
c-220.example: Sr gives red at about 650 nm, Ba green at about 520 nm, Cu blue at about 450 nm and Na yellow at about 589 nm. Blue is hardest to make because copper compounds break down easily above about 1,200 °C.
c-220.actionItem: If you watch fireworks today, try to guess the metal from each color, and keep your distance from the debris and smoke.

c-221.title: Disinfecting Water With a Clear PET Bottle and Sunshine
c-221.summary: Filling a clear PET bottle with clear water and leaving it in sunshine for 6 hours is an emergency method (SODIS) to reduce pathogens. Cloudy water must be filtered first, and it is not a perfect drinking-water treatment.
c-221.principle: UVA (320-400 nm) and heat damage the DNA and proteins of pathogens and inactivate them. The effect scales with UV dose $H=I\,t$ (intensity times time), and a water temperature above 50 °C greatly increases it.
c-221.example: On a sunny day a 1-2 L clear PET bottle left 6 hours reduces most bacteria, and under cloudy skies it needs two days. Effectiveness drops when turbidity exceeds 30 NTU.
c-221.actionItem: If you try it as an emergency test today, use only clear water and lay the bottle in sun for 6 hours, but normally prefer boiled or treated water.

c-222.title: Plastic Wrap Comes in PVC and PE, and They Differ
c-222.summary: Cling wrap comes in PVC and PE (polyethylene), and each has different safe limits for microwave use and contact with fatty foods. Check the material and heat rating on the pack.
c-222.principle: PVC wrap contains plasticizers for flexibility, which can migrate into food when it touches fatty food or is heated. PE wrap needs no plasticizer and its heat rating of about 110 °C differs from PVC's (some labeled products list 130 °C or more).
c-222.example: When microwaving, fatty food can exceed 100 °C so wrap touching it can melt or let plasticizer migrate. Keep 2-3 cm of space between wrap and food.
c-222.actionItem: Today, check the material and heat rating before using wrap, and in the microwave keep it lifted off the food.

c-223.title: When Hot Oil Touches a Styrofoam Instant-Noodle Container
c-223.summary: Putting hot, oily food in a polystyrene (Styrofoam) container can soften it and let a little styrene leach out. Follow the container's heat rating.
c-223.principle: Polystyrene softens near its glass transition at about 100 °C and dissolves readily in oil, so styrene monomer ($\mathrm{C_8H_8}$) can migrate into food. Migration rises with temperature and contact time.
c-223.example: Instant-noodle broth at about 90 °C is below polystyrene's softening point and generally acceptable, but cooking oil above 100 °C or very oily food can melt the container. Use disposable containers only once.
c-223.actionItem: Today, move hot, oily food from a Styrofoam container into a heat-resistant glass or ceramic bowl.

c-224.title: Biodegradable Plastic Bags Don't Rot at Home
c-224.summary: Most biodegradable bags break down only at the high temperatures of composting facilities and barely rot in a home garden or trash can. Follow local disposal labels.
c-224.principle: PLA (polylactic acid) hydrolyzes with water, $(\mathrm{C_3H_4O_2})_n+n\,\mathrm{H_2O}\rightarrow n\,\mathrm{C_3H_6O_3}$ (lactic acid). The reaction speeds up above the glass transition of about 58 °C, so it needs industrial composting conditions (about 58 °C and humid).
c-224.example: In an industrial composter (58 °C, moist), PLA breaks down in about 90-180 days, but in a 20 °C home it can take years or barely degrade. It doesn't break down well in the sea either.
c-224.actionItem: If you get a biodegradable-labeled bag today, sort it as general waste and, if you can, bring a reusable shopping bag instead.

c-225.title: Why Garden Hoses Crack and Crumble in the Sun
c-225.summary: A garden hose left outside gets stiffer and cracks over the years because UV in sunlight breaks polymer chains. When not in use, coil it in the shade.
c-225.principle: UV photon energy $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$ breaks C-Cl and C-H bonds in polymers such as PVC, forming radicals that react with oxygen and cut the chains. Shorter chains make the material brittle.
c-225.example: A hose with UV stabilizer lasts 3-5 years, whereas one left in constant sun can lose plasticizer and crack within 1-2 years. Midday in midsummer, when UV index is highest, is the most damaging.
c-225.actionItem: After using the hose today, drain it and coil it in shade or inside a hose reel box away from sunlight.

c-226.title: Why Rubber Bands and Rubber Gloves Crack
c-226.summary: Rubber bands and gloves suddenly crack and snap because ozone in the air attacks the rubber's double bonds. Rubber stored stretched cracks faster.
c-226.principle: Ozone adds across the C=C double bonds of natural rubber (polyisoprene), $\mathrm{C{=}C}+\mathrm{O_3}\rightarrow$ ozonide, and the bond breaks. Cracks run perpendicular to the stretch on the surface of stretched rubber.
c-226.example: Ambient ozone is typically 0.02-0.06 ppm, yet even that can crack stretched rubber in weeks to months. Storing it in a cool place extends its life considerably.
c-226.actionItem: Today, store rubber bands and gloves unstretched in a sealed bag in a cool, dark drawer.

c-227.title: Why White Sneakers Turn Yellow
c-227.summary: White sneakers yellow even in storage because polyurethane in the sole oxidizes with light and oxygen and phenolic antioxidants change. Store them in a cool, dark place.
c-227.principle: Aromatic parts of polyurethane oxidize under UV and oxygen to form yellow chromophores, and phenolic antioxidants react with nitrogen oxides to become yellow quinone-type compounds. Photo-oxidation grows with UV dose.
c-227.example: Left on a bright windowsill they can yellow noticeably within weeks to months, several times faster than in a dark shoe cabinet. The yellow forms in a thin surface layer, which oxygen bleach can partly reduce.
c-227.actionItem: Today, keep white sneakers in a dark, ventilated shoe cabinet instead of a sunny windowsill, and store them in a cotton bag rather than plastic.

c-228.title: Why New Jeans Bleed Color the First Time You Wash Them
c-228.summary: New jeans bleed blue in the first wash because indigo dye sits only on the fiber surface as particles. Wash them inside out, alone, in cold water the first time.
c-228.principle: Indigo is insoluble in water: it's dyed in a reduced soluble form, then oxidizes in air so insoluble particles cling to the fiber surface. It doesn't chemically bond to the fiber, so friction and water wash it off.
c-228.example: A new pair of jeans (about 600 g) can shed about 1-2 g of dye in the first wash, turning white clothes blue if washed together. In cold water (30 °C or below) less dye comes out.
c-228.actionItem: Today, wash new jeans alone inside out in cold water the first time, don't mix them with whites, and dry them in the shade.

c-229.title: Wet cement is alkaline and can burn your skin
c-229.summary: Wet cement and concrete are strongly alkaline, and skin left in contact can suffer chemical burns before it hurts.
c-229.principle: Calcium compounds in cement react with water to form $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ (pH about 12.5), and alkali hydrolyzes skin proteins and fats. $\mathrm{CaO + H_2O \to Ca(OH)_2}$
c-229.example: Kneeling on wet concrete for 1-2 hours has caused painless second-degree burns in reported cases. A pH of 12.5 means roughly 300,000 times more $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$ than neutral water.
c-229.actionItem: If cement touches skin, brush off dry powder first, then rinse under running water for 15+ minutes; wear waterproof gloves and long trousers for any job today.

c-230.title: Be careful with heat and gas from drain openers
c-230.summary: Lye-based drain openers heat up as they dissolve, and they release hydrogen gas if they touch aluminum.
c-230.principle: NaOH releases about 44.5 kJ/mol when dissolving, and reacts with aluminum to form hydrogen. $2\mathrm{Al} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} + 6\mathrm{H_2O} \to 2\mathrm{Na[Al(OH)_4]} + 3\mathrm{H_2}$
c-230.example: Dissolving 100 g NaOH (2.5 mol) releases about 111 kJ, enough to warm 1 L of water by about 26 °C. In a narrow pipe it can get much hotter locally and spatter.
c-230.actionItem: If you use a drain opener today, ventilate, wear goggles and gloves, and never mix it with other cleaners or put it in aluminum containers.

c-231.title: Epoxy only cures if you mix the ratio exactly
c-231.summary: Epoxy hardens fully only when resin and hardener meet in the stated ratio; otherwise it stays tacky.
c-231.principle: Epoxide groups react with amine active hydrogens in equivalent amounts to build a network. Hardener mass is $m_{\mathrm{hardener}} = \frac{\mathrm{AHEW}}{\mathrm{EEW}} \times m_{\mathrm{resin}}$.
c-231.example: With 5 mL resin and 5 mL hardener (1:1), a ratio error of 20% or more often leaves a sticky, soft result. Full cure usually takes about 24 hours.
c-231.actionItem: If you use epoxy today, measure to the label ratio, mix for at least 2 minutes while scraping the bottom, and apply a thin layer.

c-232.title: A fish tank stabilizes as ammonia turns into nitrate
c-232.summary: A new tank builds up ammonia and nitrite until nitrifying bacteria establish, which is dangerous for fish.
c-232.principle: Nitrifying bacteria convert toxic ammonia to nitrite, then to less toxic nitrate. $\mathrm{NH_4^+ + 1.5\,O_2 \to NO_2^- + 2H^+ + H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NO_2^- + 0.5\,O_2 \to NO_3^-}$
c-232.example: A new tank usually needs 4-6 weeks to cycle, and it is safest to add fish only once ammonia and nitrite read 0 ppm. Keep nitrate under 40 ppm with a 20-30% water change weekly.
c-232.actionItem: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate with a test kit today, and when changing water rinse the filter media in removed tank water, not in tap water.

c-233.title: Never pour water on a grease fire; cover it with a lid
c-233.summary: Water on burning oil sends flaming oil and steam flying in every direction.
c-233.principle: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat, so a lid cuts off oxygen. Water sinks under the oil, flashes to steam, and expands about 1,700 times. $\mathrm{H_2O(l) \to H_2O(g)}$
c-233.example: One cup (200 mL) of water hitting oil above 300 °C instantly makes about 340 L of steam, which can throw burning oil up to the ceiling.
c-233.actionItem: Today, keep a lid that fits your pan within reach of the stove, and remember the order: turn off the heat, then cover the pan.

c-234.title: Why recirculation-only on a long drive makes you sleepy
c-234.summary: Running recirculation mode for a long time lets carbon dioxide build up in the car, which can bring drowsiness and weaker focus.
c-234.principle: In a sealed cabin, exhaled CO2 cannot escape, so its concentration rises with time. $\Delta C \approx \frac{G}{V}\,t$ ($G$: generation rate, $V$: cabin volume)
c-234.example: Outdoor air holds about 420 ppm CO2, but a car with several people on recirculation for 30-60 minutes has been measured above 2,000 ppm. Drowsiness is commonly reported above about 1,000 ppm.
c-234.actionItem: On today's drive, switch to fresh-air mode or crack a window for a minute every 20-30 minutes.

c-235.title: Let the first morning tap water run for a moment
c-235.summary: Water that sat in the pipes overnight can pick up metal ions, so run the tap briefly before using it.
c-235.principle: Copper and lead in pipes and fittings slowly oxidize into the water. $\mathrm{Pb \to Pb^{2+} + 2e^-}$, $\mathrm{Cu \to Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}$ The longer it stagnates, the higher the concentration.
c-235.example: After 6+ hours of standing, run the tap 30-60 seconds until the water turns cold. At 6 L/min, a minute is about 6 L, which can go to plants or cleaning so it is not wasted.
c-235.actionItem: Tomorrow morning, run the tap 30-60 seconds before filling a cup, and collect that water for plants or mopping.

c-236.title: Alkaline water is quickly neutralized in your stomach
c-236.summary: Stomach acid neutralizes alkaline water almost immediately, so it cannot change your body's pH and is rarely worth a premium price.
c-236.principle: Gastric juice is about 0.01-0.1 M HCl (pH 1.5-3.5), and the $\mathrm{OH^-}$ in alkaline water reacts with it at once. $\mathrm{HCl + OH^- \to H_2O + Cl^-}$
c-236.example: One liter of pH 9 water has only $10^{-5}$ mol of $\mathrm{OH^-}$, enough to neutralize about 1% of 100 mL of pH 2 stomach acid ($10^{-3}$ mol H+). Blood pH is held at 7.35-7.45 by breathing and the kidneys.
c-236.actionItem: Before buying alkaline water, check for unsupported health claims; today, plain tap or filtered water is enough to hydrate.

c-237.title: Storing batteries in the fridge gains you almost nothing
c-237.summary: Modern alkaline batteries self-discharge very slowly even at room temperature, so refrigeration helps little and risks condensation.
c-237.principle: Self-discharge is chemical, so it speeds up with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation. $k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$ Cooling slows it, but alkaline cells are already very slow.
c-237.example: Alkaline batteries lose only about 2-3% per year at 20 °C, giving a shelf life of 5-10 years. A fridge saves around 1% a year, and water droplets after removal can corrode the terminals.
c-237.actionItem: Today, keep batteries in a cool, dry drawer grouped by type, and never mix new and old cells in one device.

c-238.title: Camping charcoal: briquettes, white and black charcoal differ
c-238.summary: Charcoal types differ in how fast they light, how much smoke they make and how long the heat lasts, so match the type to the job.
c-238.principle: The higher the carbonization, the less volatile matter and the more carbon, giving less smoke and longer burning. $\mathrm{C + O_2 \to CO_2}$ ($\Delta H \approx -394$ kJ/mol); with too little oxygen, $2\mathrm{C + O_2 \to 2CO}$.
c-238.example: One kg of charcoal gives about 29 MJ (about 8 kWh). White charcoal baked near 1,000 °C burns long and clean but is hard to light; black charcoal lights easily but smokes more; briquettes leave more ash because of binders.
c-238.actionItem: If you buy camping charcoal today, pick by purpose, and never burn charcoal inside a tent or closed space (carbon monoxide poisoning).

c-239.title: Why eat carbs right after exercise
c-239.summary: In the first hour or two after exercise, muscles take up sugar best, so carbohydrates then refill glycogen quickly.
c-239.principle: Glycogen emptied by exercise is rebuilt with insulin and muscle glucose transporters. $(\mathrm{Glucose})_n + \mathrm{Glucose} \to (\mathrm{Glucose})_{n+1}$
c-239.example: Muscles store about 400 g of glycogen. For a typical exerciser, a banana (about 27 g carbs) and a glass of milk after a hard workout is enough; if you rest a day or more, exact timing matters little.
c-239.actionItem: If you work out today, eat carbs with some protein within an hour afterward, such as a banana, a bowl of rice, or milk.

c-240.title: The bright color of dried apricots comes from sulfites
c-240.summary: Bright orange dried apricots are protected from browning by sulfites, while brown ones are usually unsulfured, and people with asthma should be careful.
c-240.principle: $\mathrm{SO_2}$ dissolves in water to form bisulfite, which inhibits browning enzymes and oxidation. $\mathrm{SO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HSO_3^- + H^+}$
c-240.example: Sulfured dried apricots can contain several hundred to about 2,000 mg/kg of $\mathrm{SO_2}$, and many countries require a label at 10 mg/kg or more. Sulfite-sensitive asthma patients can have breathing trouble.
c-240.actionItem: When buying dried fruit today, read the ingredient list for sulfites (sulphur dioxide), and choose brown unsulfured ones if you are sensitive.

c-241.title: Low-sodium salt is rich in potassium: caution with kidney disease
c-241.summary: Low-sodium salt swaps part of the sodium for potassium, so people with kidney disease or potassium-affecting medicines must talk to a doctor first.
c-241.principle: Part of the $\mathrm{NaCl}$ is replaced by $\mathrm{KCl}$, cutting sodium but raising potassium. By mass, Na is 39.3% of NaCl and K is 52.4% of KCl.
c-241.example: Five g of a 70% sodium / 30% potassium blend has about 1.4 g sodium (30% less than the 2.0 g in 5 g of regular salt) and about 0.79 g potassium. With reduced kidney function, potassium can build up and risk dangerous heart rhythms.
c-241.actionItem: Before buying low-sodium salt today, check the KCl share on the label, and ask your doctor first if you have kidney disease or take related medicines.

c-242.title: 14K and 18K gold are not pure gold
c-242.summary: The karat number shows gold content: 18K is 75% gold and 14K about 58%, with other metals making up the rest.
c-242.principle: Purity is expressed in 24ths. $\text{purity} = \frac{K}{24}$ Alloying makes gold harder and changes its color, while 24K pure gold is soft at about 99.9%.
c-242.example: A 10 g 18K ring holds 7.5 g of pure gold, and a 14K one about 5.8 g. Hallmarks are usually 750 for 18K and 585 for 14K.
c-242.actionItem: When buying gold today, check the hallmark (750, 585, etc.) and weight, and calculate the pure gold content yourself.

c-243.title: Coffee beans degas after roasting, then oxidize
c-243.summary: Beans release carbon dioxide right after roasting and then oxidize, so aim to drink them within about 1-4 weeks of the roast date.
c-243.principle: The $\mathrm{CO_2}$ made during roasting slowly escapes, while aroma compounds and oils react with oxygen and go stale. $\mathrm{RH + O_2 \to ROOH}$
c-243.example: One gram of beans releases several mL of CO2 after roasting, and grinding multiplies surface area so aroma fades within minutes to hours. Opened beans at room temperature noticeably lose flavor in about 2-4 weeks.
c-243.actionItem: When buying beans today, choose a bag with a roast date, grind just before brewing, and store airtight in a cool dark place (the fridge risks moisture).

c-244.title: Why the oil-repellent coating on a phone screen wears off
c-244.summary: A phone's anti-fingerprint coating is only a few to tens of nanometers thick, so it gradually wears away with wiping and abrasion.
c-244.principle: A fluoropolymer film lowers surface energy so oil beads up instead of spreading. The contact angle follows $\cos\theta = \frac{\gamma_{SV} - \gamma_{SL}}{\gamma_{LV}}$, and as the film wears, $\theta$ drops.
c-244.example: The coating is roughly a few to tens of nm thick, about one ten-thousandth of a hair's width (around 80,000 nm). Sand and keys in a pocket plus repeated alcohol cleaning wear it down visibly within months to 2 years.
c-244.actionItem: From today, wipe the screen with a dry microfiber cloth, and avoid alcohol-heavy wipes or rough cloths.

c-245.title: Take dry-cleaned clothes out of the plastic and air them
c-245.summary: Freshly dry-cleaned clothes can retain solvent, so remove the plastic and ventilate before wearing or storing them.
c-245.principle: The cleaning solvent perchloroethylene boils at 121 °C and has a vapor pressure of about 1.9 kPa at 20 °C, so it evaporates slowly. $\mathrm{C_2Cl_4(l) \to C_2Cl_4(g)}$ Plastic traps the vapor.
c-245.example: Leaving garments in plastic inside the closet traps vapor and raises odor and exposure. Hanging them in a breezy place for several hours to a day lets most escape. Some cleaners use hydrocarbon solvents instead.
c-245.actionItem: Take clothes out of the plastic as soon as you bring them home from the cleaner, and hang them for several hours on a balcony or in a ventilated spot.

c-246.title: A condensing boiler recovers heat from the water vapor in exhaust
c-246.summary: A condensing boiler condenses the water vapor in its exhaust and uses that latent heat for heating, instead of throwing it away.
c-246.principle: Burning natural gas makes water, $\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \to CO_2 + 2H_2O}$, and condensing that vapor releases latent heat of about 2.26 MJ/kg. To recover it, the return water should be below about 55 °C.
c-246.example: Burning 1 m³ of gas makes about 1.6 kg of water, adding roughly 3.6 MJ (about 10% of the total heat). That is why it can save about 10-15% energy versus a conventional boiler.
c-246.actionItem: If you use a condensing boiler today, lower the heating setpoint so return water stays below 55 °C and condensation works well.

c-247.title: A candle burns vaporized wax, not melted wax
c-247.summary: A candle flame burns wax vapor drawn up the wick, not the liquid wax itself.
c-247.principle: Melted wax climbs the wick by capillary action, vaporizes in the heat, and the vapor reacts with oxygen. $\mathrm{C_{25}H_{52} + 38\,O_2 \to 25\,CO_2 + 26\,H_2O}$
c-247.example: An ordinary candle burns about 7 g of wax per hour and gives off roughly 80 W of heat. A wick that is too long burns incompletely and makes more soot.
c-247.actionItem: Before lighting a candle today, trim the wick to about 5 mm to cut soot, and never leave a lit candle unattended.

c-248.title: Boiling pasta in less water cuts energy use
c-248.summary: Pasta needs only about 1 L of water per 100 g, so switching from a habit of boiling 3 L cuts the heat needed a lot.
c-248.principle: Heating water takes $Q = mc\Delta T$, and pasta starch absorbs water and gelatinizes from about 60-70 °C, so a huge pot is unnecessary.
c-248.example: Raising 1 L of water from 20 °C to 100 °C takes about 334 kJ (0.093 kWh), so cutting from 3 L to 1 L saves about 0.19 kWh each time. Using a lid saves even more.
c-248.actionItem: When cooking pasta today, use only about 1 L of water per 100 g, put a lid on while heating, and stir often so it doesn't stick.

c-249.title: Ventilate first when a fluorescent lamp breaks
c-249.summary: Fluorescent lamps contain a little mercury, so when one breaks, move people and pets out and ventilate before cleaning up.
c-249.principle: Mercury is a metal that evaporates even at room temperature. $\mathrm{Hg(l) \to Hg(g)}$ Its vapor pressure at 20 °C is about 0.16 Pa, and the vapor builds up in a closed room.
c-249.example: One compact fluorescent lamp (CFL) usually holds a few mg of mercury. After a break, ventilate for 5-10+ minutes, and collect the pieces with stiff paper and tape instead of a vacuum, then seal them for a collection bin.
c-249.actionItem: Today, find any spent fluorescent tubes at home, put them in their original box, and learn where the nearest lamp collection bin is.

c-250.title: Use less water for new-crop rice than for old rice
c-250.summary: New-crop rice holds more moisture, so use about 90% of your usual water or the rice turns mushy.
c-250.principle: The older rice gets, the drier it is and the more water it absorbs. Cooking water is roughly $m_{\mathrm{water}} = m_{\mathrm{rice}} \times r$, with $r$ about 1.1 for new rice and 1.2 for old.
c-250.example: For 2 cups (about 360 mL) of rice you might use about 400 mL of water, but with new rice use about 360 mL, roughly 40 mL less. New rice is about 15-16% moisture, old rice 13-14%.
c-250.actionItem: When cooking new-crop rice today, use about 90% of your usual water, and cut back more next time if it is mushy.

c-251.title: Mix pancake batter briefly in cold water for crispness
c-251.summary: Korean-style jeon batter turns crisp when mixed briefly with cold water, which limits chewy gluten.
c-251.principle: Glutenin and gliadin in flour form a gluten network when wet and agitated. $\text{glutenin} + \text{gliadin} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{mixing}} \text{gluten}$ Cold water slows this down.
c-251.example: Stir 1 cup (about 120 g) of flour with 1 cup of cold water for only about 10 strokes; small lumps are fine. Replacing about 20% of the flour with starch dilutes gluten for extra crispness.
c-251.actionItem: If you make savory pancakes today, mix with ice-cold water for only 10-15 seconds, and don't keep stirring the batter for 10+ minutes.

c-252.title: Bracken fiddleheads need blanching and soaking to cut toxins
c-252.summary: Raw bracken contains a carcinogen called ptaquiloside, so always boil and soak it, and still avoid eating it very often.
c-252.principle: Ptaquiloside breaks down with heat and alkali. $\text{ptaquiloside} \xrightarrow{\Delta,\ \mathrm{OH^-}} \text{pterosin B}$ (non-toxic)
c-252.example: Boil for 5-10 minutes, then soak in cold water for about a day; adding about 5 g (0.5%) baking soda per 1 L of water helps breakdown. It does not guarantee zero, so don't eat it often or in large amounts.
c-252.actionItem: If you cook bracken today, boil it thoroughly, soak it in cold water, and only then prepare the dish.

c-253.title: Why taro makes your hands itch, and the fix
c-253.summary: Taro skin and juice contain needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals that sting and itch bare hands.
c-253.principle: Calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) pierce skin to cause itching, and they partly dissolve or lose effect in acid or heat. $\mathrm{CaC_2O_4 + 2H^+ \rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+} + H_2C_2O_4}$
c-253.example: The crystals are tens to hundreds of micrometers long (0.02-0.2 mm), sharp enough to pierce the outer skin layer. For itching, rinsing in warm water with a little vinegar can help, and boiling greatly reduces the acrid taste.
c-253.actionItem: When preparing taro today, wear rubber gloves and peel it under running water.

c-254.title: Pine needles help songpyeon keep a bit longer as a natural preservative
c-254.summary: The terpenes in the pine needles under songpyeon have a mild antibacterial effect, but they are not a preservative, so storage still matters.
c-254.principle: Terpenes like alpha-pinene ($\mathrm{C_{10}H_{16}}$) disturb bacterial cell membranes and slow growth. The effect is weak and extends keeping time only by hours to about a day.
c-254.example: Songpyeon usually lasts about a day at cool room temperature; in the fridge the rice cake hardens (retrogradation); frozen it keeps about 1 month. Relying on the pine needles alone at summer room temperature can lead to spoilage.
c-254.actionItem: Today, cool leftover songpyeon, wrap each one in plastic wrap and freeze it, then steam to reheat before eating.

c-255.title: Red ginseng is steamed, so its saponin structure has changed
c-255.summary: Red ginseng is fresh ginseng steamed and dried, and steaming strips sugars off ginseng saponins (ginsenosides), creating compounds found only in red ginseng.
c-255.principle: Steam heat and moisture hydrolyze the sugar chains of ginsenosides. $\text{Rb}_1 \xrightarrow{\text{steam, H}^+} \text{Rg}_3 + 2\ \text{glucose}$
c-255.example: Red ginseng is made by steaming fresh ginseng at about 95-100 °C for hours and then drying, which produces compounds such as Rg3, Rg5 and Rk1. Health benefits cannot be assumed, and ginsenoside content varies by product.
c-255.actionItem: When buying a red ginseng product today, compare the root age (such as 6-year) and the labeled ginsenoside content (Rg1+Rb1+Rg3 total).

c-256.title: The white powder on grape skin is not pesticide
c-256.summary: The dusty white coating on grapes is natural wax (bloom) the fruit makes itself, and it is also a sign of freshness.
c-256.principle: Bloom is hydrophobic wax crystals such as oleanolic acid ($\mathrm{C_{30}H_{48}O_3}$), a natural waterproof layer that slows water loss and blocks mold and rain.
c-256.example: The bloom layer is only a few micrometers thick or less and rubs off easily with a finger. An even bloom suggests the grapes were handled little since harvest, which helps judge freshness.
c-256.actionItem: Today, rinse grapes under running water for 30 seconds just before eating, and don't wash them in advance.

c-257.title: Autumn leaves turn red because the leaf makes new pigment
c-257.summary: Yellow leaves reveal pigment that was already there, while red leaves make new anthocyanin in autumn.
c-257.principle: As days shorten and cool, chlorophyll ($\mathrm{C_{55}H_{72}O_5N_4Mg}$) breaks down, exposing yellow carotenoids, and as sugar accumulates, anthocyanin is newly synthesized, turning leaves red.
c-257.example: Reds are most vivid with sunny days that build sugar and mornings dropping to 5-10 °C. In a rainy, warm autumn, colors are duller.
c-257.actionItem: If you plan a foliage trip today, check the foliage forecast map for 1-2 weeks after morning lows start hovering around 5 °C.

c-258.title: Don't pick up ginkgo fruit with bare hands
c-258.summary: The pulp of ginkgo fruit can cause a rash like poison ivy on bare skin, and the smell comes from butyric acid.
c-258.principle: Ginkgolic acids (alkylphenols) in the pulp cause contact dermatitis, and the foul odor is butyric acid. $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2COOH}$
c-258.example: Pulp juice on skin can lead to red rash and itching hours to a day later. Butyric acid is the same family of smell as rancid butter or vomit.
c-258.actionItem: On today's autumn walk, don't pick up fallen ginkgo fruit, and if you must, wear disposable gloves and handle it inside a bag.

c-259.title: Boiling or drying doesn't remove poisonous mushroom toxins
c-259.summary: Toxins of poisonous mushrooms survive boiling, drying and the silver spoon test, so never eat wild mushrooms that an expert hasn't identified.
c-259.principle: The amatoxin (alpha-amanitin) of death caps is a heat-stable cyclic peptide that blocks RNA polymerase II and damages liver and kidney cells. $\text{amatoxin} + \text{RNA polymerase II} \to \text{inactive complex}$
c-259.example: The lethal dose is about 0.1 mg/kg, so a single death cap (about 50 g) can be fatal to an adult. Symptoms appear only after 6-24 hours, making it easy to get help too late.
c-259.actionItem: If you meet wild mushrooms on a hike today, don't pick them, and if you ate some and have vomiting or diarrhea, go to the ER at once and bring the mushroom.

c-260.title: Why you shouldn't burn autumn leaves and trash
c-260.summary: Burning leaves and trash outdoors burns incompletely and releases fine dust and harmful compounds, and burning plastic or PVC can make dioxins.
c-260.principle: Open burning with limited oxygen is incomplete combustion, giving PAHs and carbon monoxide. $2\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \to 2\mathrm{CO}$ PVC $(\mathrm{C_2H_3Cl})_n$ can form hydrogen chloride and dioxin-type compounds when burned.
c-260.example: About 57% of PVC's mass is chlorine, so 1 kg holds about 570 g of chlorine. Open burning of crop residue can emit roughly 5-15 g of fine particles per kg.
c-260.actionItem: Today, don't burn leaves; compost them or put them out following your local collection rules.

c-261.title: The white powder from humidifiers is tap-water minerals
c-261.summary: The white dust that settles around an ultrasonic humidifier is the calcium and magnesium minerals dissolved in your tap water.
c-261.principle: An ultrasonic humidifier sprays fine droplets without boiling, so dissolved salts stay behind as solid particles when the droplets dry. Boiling lets some hardness settle out. $\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \to CaCO_3 + CO_2 + H_2O}$
c-261.example: With about 80 mg/L of minerals in tap water and 2.4 L sprayed over an 8-hour night, roughly 190 mg of particles can spread into the air. These are small enough to reach the airways.
c-261.actionItem: Today, empty, rinse and refill the humidifier tank daily, and where possible use distilled water or a heated or evaporative model.

c-262.title: Why old books turn yellow
c-262.summary: Old books yellow and crumble because acids and lignin in the paper oxidize and break down.
c-262.principle: Lignin in acidic paper oxidizes with light and oxygen and turns yellow, and acid hydrolyzes cellulose to weaken the paper. $(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}O_5})_n + n\mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} n\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$
c-262.example: Lignin-rich paper like newsprint (about 25% lignin) yellows in months, while acid-free books can last centuries. Higher humidity and temperature speed the reactions up.
c-262.actionItem: Today, shelve valued books away from direct sunlight in a cool dry spot, and don't tuck newspaper clippings between pages.

c-263.title: Black rot at the base of tomatoes comes from calcium
c-263.summary: The black rot at the bottom of tomatoes (blossom-end rot) is usually less about missing calcium in the soil and more about calcium not reaching the fruit.
c-263.principle: Calcium ions travel with the water stream driven by transpiration, and the fruit tip, which transpires little, gets it last. Slow flow means less supply. $J = C \times \dot{V}$ ($C$: calcium concentration, $\dot{V}$: water flow)
c-263.example: Uneven watering interrupts calcium movement and triggers symptoms; steady watering of about 25 mm (1 inch) of water per week is commonly advised. Managing water works better than adding lots of calcium to the soil.
c-263.actionItem: Today, water tomatoes at a steady interval before the soil dries out instead of in irregular bursts, and add mulch.

c-264.title: Charcoal-fire ash is free potassium for the garden, with cautions
c-264.summary: Wood ash is an alkaline fertilizer supplying potassium and calcium, but it harms acid-loving plants, and ash from additive-laden briquettes or painted wood must not be used.
c-264.principle: The $\mathrm{K_2CO_3}$ in ash dissolves into potassium and hydroxide ions, raising soil pH. $\mathrm{K_2CO_3 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons 2K^+ + HCO_3^- + OH^-}$
c-264.example: Wood ash has a pH of 10-13 and about 3-10% potassium (as K2O). A common limit is about 100 g per m² per year (a couple of handfuls), and avoid blueberries and potatoes.
c-264.actionItem: If you have fully cooled, pure wood ash today, sift it, test your soil pH, and spread a thin layer only on neutral to alkaline beds.

c-265.title: If your compost smells bad, add carbon
c-265.summary: If compost smells of ammonia or rot, it has too much nitrogen, so mix in carbon materials such as dry leaves.
c-265.principle: Microbes work best at a carbon to nitrogen ratio of about 30:1. $\mathrm{C/N} = \frac{m_C}{m_N} \approx 30$ Excess nitrogen escapes as ammonia smell via $\mathrm{NH_4^+ + OH^- \to NH_3 + H_2O}$.
c-265.example: Food scraps have a C/N of about 15-20, dry leaves 50-80 and sawdust about 400. Mixing 2-3 parts by volume of browns like dry leaves with 1 part food scraps greatly cuts the smell.
c-265.actionItem: If your compost bin smells today, add a bag of dry leaves or shredded cardboard, and mix well to aerate it.

c-266.title: Undercooked kidney beans carry lectin toxicity
c-266.summary: Raw kidney beans, or beans only warmed to about 80 °C, can cause vomiting and diarrhea from lectins, so they must be boiled hard.
c-266.principle: Kidney bean lectin (phytohaemagglutinin) is a protein that only denatures with sufficient heat at 100 °C. $\text{active lectin} \xrightarrow{100^\circ\mathrm{C},\ \ge 10\ \text{min}} \text{denatured lectin}$ At about 80 °C, toxicity can actually rise severalfold.
c-266.example: As few as 4-5 raw red kidney beans can cause nausea and vomiting within 1-3 hours, and low-temperature 80 °C cooking has been reported to raise toxicity about 5 times above raw beans. Canned beans are already cooked.
c-266.actionItem: If you cook dried kidney beans today, soak 5+ hours, discard the water, boil vigorously for at least 10 minutes, then simmer.

c-267.title: Don't screw the plum syrup jar lid on tight
c-267.summary: Plum syrup ferments with yeast and gives off carbon dioxide, so a tightly sealed jar can build pressure and burst.
c-267.principle: Yeast breaks sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \to 2\,C_2H_5OH + 2\,CO_2}$
c-267.example: Fermenting just 10 g of glucose (about 0.056 mol) releases about 2.7 L of CO2, so pressure can rise fast in a 3 L jar. It happens more when sugar is undissolved or the weather is warm.
c-267.actionItem: Today, set the plum syrup jar lid loosely or cover with cloth, and if it foams, open the lid once a day to vent gas.

c-268.title: Why washing curry stains with soap turns them red
c-268.summary: Curry's yellow pigment (curcumin) turns red in alkali, so scrubbing with alkaline soap makes the stain redder and darker.
c-268.principle: Curcumin is a pH indicator: yellow in acidic to neutral conditions and reddish-brown above about pH 8.6. $\mathrm{HCur \rightleftharpoons H^+ + Cur^-}$ (yellow ⇌ red)
c-268.example: Bar soap solution has a pH of 9-10, beyond that color change. A neutral dish detergent (about pH 7) doesn't shift the color, and drying in sunlight photodegrades curcumin so it fades.
c-268.actionItem: If you get a curry stain today, rinse with cold water, dab with neutral dish detergent, skip the soap, and dry it in the sun.

c-269.title: Why hard-boiled yolks get a greenish ring
c-269.summary: The green ring on overcooked hard-boiled yolks is harmless iron sulfide, and shorter cooking prevents it.
c-269.principle: Hydrogen sulfide released from sulfur amino acids in the white reacts with iron in the yolk to form iron sulfide. $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + H_2S \to FeS + 2H^+}$
c-269.example: A large egg is fully hard-boiled about 10-12 minutes after the water starts boiling, and past about 15 minutes a green ring easily forms. Chilling in cold water for 5 minutes right away stops the reaction.
c-269.actionItem: When boiling eggs today, cook only 10-12 minutes after boiling starts, then cool immediately in cold water for 5 minutes.

c-270.title: Swallowing a button battery can burn within 2 hours
c-270.summary: A swallowed coin-shaped button battery can cause severe burns in the esophagus within 2 hours, so go to the ER immediately even without symptoms.
c-270.principle: When the battery touches saliva in the esophagus, current flows and electrolyzes water, producing hydroxide at the negative side and a strongly alkaline burn. $2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \to \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}$
c-270.example: A 20 mm, 3 V lithium button cell (CR2032) easily lodges in a child's esophagus, and tissue pH can reach 12-13. Damage starts within 2 hours, and you must not induce vomiting or wait it out.
c-270.actionItem: Today, check that the battery compartments of remotes, key fobs and toys are screwed shut, and keep spare cells out of children's reach.

c-271.title: Limit tuna and swordfish to 1-2 times a week because of mercury
c-271.summary: Large predatory fish like tuna and swordfish concentrate methylmercury, so it is wise to limit them to about 1-2 servings a week.
c-271.principle: Microbes convert mercury into methylmercury, which accumulates up the food chain. $\mathrm{Hg^{2+} \xrightarrow{\text{microbes}} CH_3Hg^+}$ The EFSA tolerable weekly intake is 1.3 μg per kg of body weight.
c-271.example: For a 60 kg person the weekly limit is 78 μg. A 100 g portion of swordfish at 1.0 ppm holds about 100 μg and can exceed it in one meal, while 100 g of light tuna at about 0.1 ppm has about 10 μg. Pregnant people and children should be stricter.
c-271.actionItem: Today, keep tuna, swordfish and shark to about 100 g per serving, and plan no more than 1-2 servings of such large fish this week.

c-272.title: Shrimp and crab turn red when cooked
c-272.summary: Shrimp and crab turn red because heat changes their proteins and releases trapped red pigment, which is a good sign they are cooked.
c-272.principle: Alive, astaxanthin is bound to protein (crustacyanin) and looks blue-gray; heat denatures the protein and frees red astaxanthin. $\text{astaxanthin-protein (blue-gray)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{astaxanthin (red)} + \text{denatured protein}$
c-272.example: Shrimp is done at an internal temperature of 63 °C (145 °F), turning opaque and pink, and 2-3 minutes in boiling water is enough. Cooking longer makes the flesh rubbery.
c-272.actionItem: When boiling shrimp today, lift them out as soon as they turn opaque pink and curl into a C shape, so they don't turn tough.

c-273.title: Old brake fluid weakens braking
c-273.summary: Brake fluid absorbs moisture from the air, lowering its boiling point, and it can boil during hard braking such as long downhills and weaken braking.
c-273.principle: Glycol-based brake fluid is hygroscopic, so water lowers its boiling point and vapor forms; vapor compresses and cannot transmit braking force. $\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$
c-273.example: DOT 4 fluid has a dry boiling point of at least 230 °C, but with absorbed water it can fall to 155 °C, a drop of about 75 °C. It typically absorbs about 2-3% water a year, so replacement every 2 years or 40,000 km is advised.
c-273.actionItem: Today, check your service record for the last brake fluid change, and if it was over 2 years ago, book a brake fluid check at a shop.

c-274.title: The pink of ham gift sets comes from nitrite curing
c-274.summary: Ham stays pink after cooking because of color made by nitrite, and it is wise not to eat much processed meat.
c-274.principle: In acid, nitrite becomes nitric oxide (NO), which binds the iron of the meat pigment myoglobin and makes pink nitrosomyoglobin. $\mathrm{NO + Mb(Fe^{2+}) \to Mb(Fe^{2+})\text{-}NO}$
c-274.example: Korea's residual nitrite limit in meat products is 70 mg/kg or less. The WHO classifies processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, estimating about 18% higher colorectal cancer risk for 50 g eaten daily.
c-274.actionItem: Refrigerate any ham gift set you receive today, and eat it in portions of about 50 g with vegetables.

c-275.title: White Powder on Dried Persimmons Is Sugar Crystals, Not Mold
c-275.summary: The pale bloom on dried persimmons is usually crystallized sugar (glucose and fructose), not mold. Fuzzy green or black spots are mold, so discard those.
c-275.principle: As the fruit dries, water leaves and sugar concentration rises. Once it passes the saturation solubility, sugar crystallizes out: $C > C_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)$, where $C=\frac{m_{\mathrm{sugar}}}{V_{\mathrm{water}}}$ grows because the denominator shrinks.
c-275.example: A fresh persimmon is about 80% water and about 15% sugar, but a dried one falls to roughly 25-30% water and 60% or more sugar by weight. That concentration is what forms the white surface bloom.
c-275.actionItem: When buying dried persimmons today, pick ones with an even, firm, dry bloom and avoid any with fuzzy green spots or sticky patches.

c-276.title: The Burning Smell When You First Turn On a Heater Is Burning Dust
c-276.summary: The musty burnt smell when you first switch on a heater after summer is often dust that settled on it being thermally decomposed. It usually fades in minutes with ventilation, but if it persists, get it checked.
c-276.principle: Organic matter in dust (fibers, skin flakes) pyrolyzes when heated, releasing volatiles and char. This starts at roughly $T \approx 150\text{~}250\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and heating element surfaces run much hotter than that.
c-276.example: An electric heater element commonly reaches 300-800°C at the surface, so dust burns easily. A 1-2 kW heater can smell for the first 30 minutes, and after cleaning the smell nearly disappears.
c-276.actionItem: Before turning your heater on today, unplug it, vacuum the intake and floor dust, then open a window and run it for 10 minutes. If the burning smell persists or smoke appears, switch it off and have it inspected.

c-277.title: Salting Napa Cabbage Wilts It and Lets Kimchi Flavor Soak In
c-277.summary: Salting cabbage draws out water by osmosis, so it wilts, takes up seasoning well, and stays crunchy. Under-salted cabbage makes bland, soggy kimchi.
c-277.principle: Cell membranes are semipermeable, so when the outside salt concentration is higher, water moves out of the cells. Osmotic pressure is $\Pi = iCRT$, and calcium cross-links pectin, keeping the tissue firm.
c-277.example: Salting one napa cabbage (about 2.5 kg) with about 200 g of salt (roughly 8%) for 4-6 hours cuts its weight by 20-25%, releasing about 0.5-0.6 kg of water. A final salt level around 2% is about right.
c-277.actionItem: If you make kimchi today, turn the cabbage once while brining, and rinse and drain it when the stem bends without snapping.

c-278.title: Astringent Persimmons Stop Being Astringent When Soluble Tannins Turn Insoluble
c-278.summary: A persimmon's puckery taste comes from water-soluble tannins, and it fades once they become insoluble. Drying or deastringency treatments rely on exactly this.
c-278.principle: Soluble tannins bind proteins in saliva and on the tongue, giving the dry feeling. As the fruit ripens, dries or is sealed, acetaldehyde ($\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$) forms and polymerizes tannins into insoluble clumps that no longer dissolve in saliva.
c-278.example: An astringent persimmon holds roughly 1% soluble tannin, which dries your mouth, but sealed at about 20-25°C for 3-5 days most of it becomes insoluble and the puckery taste nearly vanishes.
c-278.actionItem: If you have astringent persimmons today, seal them in a container or bag with an apple or banana for 2-3 days, or peel and sun-dry them. Taste a small piece before eating to check.

c-279.title: Grapefruit Juice Can Change How Some Medicines Work
c-279.summary: Grapefruit can block the breakdown of some drugs, raising their levels in the blood. If you take any medication, ask a pharmacist whether grapefruit interacts with it.
c-279.principle: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit inhibit the intestinal drug-metabolizing enzyme CYP3A4. With less breakdown, more drug is absorbed, so $AUC=\int_0^\infty C(t)\,dt$ rises and side-effect risk increases.
c-279.example: For some statins, one glass (about 250 mL) of grapefruit juice can multiply blood exposure (AUC) several-fold, and the effect can last more than a day. The size of the effect varies a lot between drugs.
c-279.actionItem: Today, check the leaflet of any medicine you take or ask a pharmacist whether grapefruit is a concern, and if so, avoid the juice and fresh fruit. Do not stop a medicine on your own.

c-280.title: Why Liquids Must Be in 100 mL Containers in Cabin Baggage
c-280.summary: On international flights, liquids and gels in carry-on bags must be in containers of 100 mL or less, packed in a clear zip bag. The limit is meant to keep any single container below a dangerous quantity.
c-280.principle: The rule limits container size because liquid explosives are only dangerous above a certain quantity. The carried total is $V_{\mathrm{total}}=\sum V_i$ with each $V_i \le 100\,\mathrm{mL}$, usually capped at one 1 L bag.
c-280.example: Ten 100 mL containers in one 1 L bag give a maximum total of about 1 L. A 200 mL bottle, even half empty, is often rejected because the container capacity is what counts.
c-280.actionItem: If you are preparing for a trip today, decant shampoo, lotion and liquid medicine into 100 mL or smaller bottles, put them in one clear zip bag, and keep it at the top of your bag. Check the airline and country rules again before departure.

c-281.title: Choose Fermented Seafood by Aging and Amino-Acid Flavor, Not Just Saltiness
c-281.summary: The savory depth of jeotgal comes from amino acids released as proteins break down during aging. Check that it is not just salty and that the production and aging details are clear.
c-281.principle: Protease enzymes in the fish gut hydrolyze protein into peptides and amino acids: $\text{protein} + n\,\mathrm{H_2O} \to n\,\text{amino acids}$. Glutamic acid in particular gives the savory umami taste.
c-281.example: Salted shrimp usually has a salt level around 20%, and after 3-6 months of aging its amino nitrogen rises and the flavor deepens. At the same salt level, a short-aged product tastes fishy and merely salty.
c-281.actionItem: When buying jeotgal today, check the production date, ingredients and salt level on the label, and if you can taste, pick the one that leaves sweetness and richness after the saltiness.

c-282.title: Check Gas Connections With Soapy Water Bubbles, Not by Smell Alone
c-282.summary: To check a suspected gas leak at a connection, brush on soapy water and watch for bubbles. Never use a flame or lighter to check, as it risks an explosion.
c-282.principle: Leaking gas pushes up the soap film formed by surfactant and makes bubbles. For a bubble, $\Delta P = \frac{4\gamma}{r}$, so even a small leak shows up as a visible bubble.
c-282.example: Brush a mix of about 1 mL dish soap in 100 mL of water onto a stove hose connection, and bubbles that keep growing or forming mean a leak. Natural gas is lighter than air and rises, while LPG is heavier and settles low.
c-282.actionItem: Today, with the gas valve closed, brush soapy water on hose connections and look for bubbles. If bubbles keep growing, shut the valve, ventilate and have a professional inspect it.

c-283.title: Chestnuts Stored Cold Get Sweeter as Starch Turns Into Sugar
c-283.summary: Fresh chestnuts kept in the fridge at 0-4°C for a few weeks turn starch into sugar and taste sweeter. At room temperature they spoil fast, so refrigeration is the thrifty choice.
c-283.principle: In the cold, amylase and other enzymes break starch into maltose and glucose: $(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}O_5})_n + n\,\mathrm{H_2O}\to n\,\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$. Plants build up sugars to protect against freezing through osmotic protection.
c-283.example: Freshly harvested chestnuts hold about 5-8% sugar, but after 4-8 weeks at 0-2°C the sugar content can rise about 1.5-2 times, giving a clearly sweeter taste. At room temperature, worms and mold appear within about two weeks.
c-283.actionItem: Today, wrap whole chestnuts in paper towels, put them in a zip bag in the fridge (about 1-4°C), and steam or roast them within 1-2 weeks.

c-284.title: Whether Home Canning Is Safe Depends on the pH 4.6 Threshold
c-284.summary: In home canning, you must separate high-acid foods at pH 4.6 or below from low-acid foods above it. Boiling-water heating alone can leave a botulism toxin risk in low-acid foods.
c-284.principle: Botulinum spores can produce toxin in sealed, oxygen-free conditions when pH is above 4.6. Acidity is $\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]$, and pH 4.6 corresponds to $[\mathrm{H^+}]\approx 2.5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$.
c-284.example: Jam and fruit preserves have a pH around 3-4, so boiling-water processing is relatively safe, but vegetables, meat and beans sit at pH 5-7 and need pressure heating at about 116-121°C. Boiling water cannot exceed 100°C.
c-284.actionItem: If you do home canning today, check whether the ingredient is acidic (fruit or vinegar pickle), and for low-acid foods refrigerate or freeze instead of canning at home. If a lid bulges or there are bubbles or an off smell, do not eat it and throw it away.

c-285.title: Chocolate Can Be Poisonous to Dogs
c-285.summary: The theobromine in chocolate is broken down slowly by dogs and can cause poisoning. The higher the cocoa content, the greater the risk, so if a dog ate some, note the type and amount and call a vet.
c-285.principle: Theobromine ($\mathrm{C_7H_8N_4O_2}$) has a half-life of about 17 hours in dogs versus about 6-10 hours in humans, so it accumulates. Risk is gauged by dose per body weight $D=\frac{m_{\mathrm{theobromine}}}{m_{\mathrm{body}}}$.
